/// A circular fence: where it is, how big, and when it counted.
///
/// Activation is **time-versioned** and geometry is not. Asking "was this
/// fence active at the fix's event time" keeps a recompute pure, so
/// deactivating a fence never rewrites the history it was part of. Moving one
/// does — see `recomputeAllGeofences` — which is the trade documented as
/// ARCHITECTURE.md §10, ambiguity 9.
class Geofence {
  const Geofence({
    required this.geofenceId,
    required this.name,
    required this.lat,
    required this.lon,
    required this.radiusM,
    required this.activeFrom,
    required this.updatedAt,
    this.activeTo,
  });

  final String geofenceId;
  final String name;
  final double lat;
  final double lon;
  final double radiusM;

  /// From when this fence starts judging fixes.
  final DateTime activeFrom;

  /// When it stopped, or null while it is live. Deactivated fences are kept,
  /// not deleted: a trip that ended at a depot has to be able to name it long
  /// after the depot closed.
  final DateTime? activeTo;

  final DateTime updatedAt;

  bool get isActive => activeTo == null;

  /// A copy with [activeTo] set or cleared, for the deactivate toggle.
  Geofence withActive({required bool active, required DateTime at}) => Geofence(
    geofenceId: geofenceId,
    name: name,
    lat: lat,
    lon: lon,
    radiusM: radiusM,
    // Reactivating starts a *new* active window rather than resuming the old
    // one, so the period it was off stays genuinely off in any recompute.
    activeFrom: active ? at : activeFrom,
    activeTo: active ? null : at,
    updatedAt: at,
  );
}

/// A fence plus how many vehicles are inside it right now.
class GeofenceOccupancy {
  const GeofenceOccupancy({required this.fence, required this.vehiclesInside});

  final Geofence fence;

  /// Counted from `geofence_containment`, not from the log.
  final int vehiclesInside;
}

/// One crossing, as the vehicle screen shows it.

  const GeofenceVisit({
    required this.geofenceName,
    required this.isEntry,
    required this.at,
    required this.isConfident,
  });

  final String geofenceName;

  /// Entry when true, exit when false.
  final bool isEntry;

  /// Event time of the first fix of the confirming pair — when the vehicle
  /// crossed, not when we became sure.
  final DateTime at;

  /// False when the confirming pair straddled a reporting gap longer than
  /// half an hour. The crossing happened; its timing is a guess.
  final bool isConfident;
}

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:get/get.dart';

import '../../domain/entities/geofence.dart';
import '../controllers/geofence_controller.dart';
import '../widgets/geofence_tile.dart';
import 'geofence_editor_page.dart';

/// The fences, with how many vehicles are in each right now.
class GeofencesPage extends GetView<GeofenceController> {
  const GeofencesPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: const Text('Geofences'),
        bottom: PreferredSize(
          preferredSize: const Size.fromHeight(4),
          child: Obx(
            () => controller.isSaving.value
                ? const LinearProgressIndicator(minHeight: 4)
                : const SizedBox(height: 4),
          ),
        ),
      ),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton.extended(
        onPressed: () => _edit(context, controller.blank(), isNew: true),
        icon: const Icon(Icons.add_location_alt_outlined),
        label: const Text('New'),
      ),
      body: Obx(() {
        if (controller.error.isNotEmpty) {
          return Center(child: Text(controller.error.value));
        }
        if (controller.isLoading.value) {
          return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
        }
        if (controller.fences.isEmpty) {
          return const Center(child: Text('No geofences yet.'));
        }

        return ListView.separated(
          itemCount: controller.fences.length,
          separatorBuilder: (_, __) => const Divider(height: 1),
          itemBuilder: (_, index) {
            final occupancy = controller.fences[index];
            return GeofenceTile(
              occupancy: occupancy,
              onEdit: () => _edit(context, occupancy.fence, isNew: false),
              onToggleActive: () => _toggle(context, occupancy.fence),
            );
          },
        );
      }),
    );
  }

  /// Opens the editor and saves what comes back.
  ///
  /// The editor is a pure form — it returns a fence and owns no writes — so
  /// the save, its progress and its failure all live on one side of the
  /// boundary.
  Future<void> _edit(
    BuildContext context,
    Geofence fence, {
    required bool isNew,
  }) async {
    final edited = await Navigator.of(context).push<Geofence>(
      MaterialPageRoute(
        builder: (_) => GeofenceEditorPage(fence: fence, isNew: isNew),
      ),
    );
    if (edited == null || !context.mounted) return;

    final messenger = ScaffoldMessenger.of(context);
    if (await controller.save(edited)) {
      messenger.showSnackBar(SnackBar(content: Text('${edited.name} saved')));
    }
  }

  /// Deactivating asks first. It is reversible and deletes nothing, but it
  /// stops a fence judging fixes from this moment on, and that gap stays in
  /// the history afterwards.
  Future<void> _toggle(BuildContext context, Geofence fence) async {
    if (fence.isActive) {
      final confirmed = await showDialog<bool>(
        context: context,
        builder: (dialogContext) => AlertDialog(
          title: Text('Deactivate ${fence.name}?'),
          content: const Text(
            'It stops tracking entries and exits from now on. Crossings '
            'already recorded are kept, and you can turn it back on.',
          ),
          actions: [
            TextButton(
              onPressed: () => Navigator.of(dialogContext).pop(false),
              child: const Text('Cancel'),
            ),
            FilledButton(
              onPressed: () => Navigator.of(dialogContext).pop(true),
              child: const Text('Deactivate'),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      );
      if (confirmed != true) return;
    }
    await controller.setActive(fence.geofenceId, active: !fence.isActive);
  }
}

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dart_duckdb/dart_duckdb.dart';
import 'package:dart_duckdb/open.dart';

/// dart_duckdb loads its native library out of the app bundle on device. Under
/// `flutter test` the host VM has loaded nothing, and the package's own test
/// fallback points at paths inside the dart_duckdb monorepo — so point it at
/// the host copy fetched by `tool/fetch_duckdb_lib.sh`.
///
/// Spawned isolates need no equivalent call: once this isolate has opened the
/// library its symbols are in the process, which is the first thing
/// dart_duckdb looks for.
void useHostDuckDb() {
  final (os, name) = Platform.isMacOS
      ? (OperatingSystem.macOS, 'libduckdb.dylib')
      : (OperatingSystem.linux, 'libduckdb.so');
  final lib = File('.duckdb/$name');
  if (!lib.existsSync()) {
    throw StateError('${lib.path} missing — run tool/fetch_duckdb_lib.sh');
  }
  open.overrideFor(os, lib.absolute.path);
}

/// ARCHITECTURE.md leans on a handful of DuckDB features. If a version bump
/// ever removes or changes one, this file fails instead of the whole app
/// quietly going wrong.
void main() {
  setUpAll(useHostDuckDb);

  late FleetDb db;
  setUp(() async => db = await FleetDb.open(':memory:'));
  tearDown(() => db.close());

  Future<List<List<Object?>>> rows(String sql) async =>
      (await db.read.query(sql)).fetchAll();

  test('natural-key PK makes duplicate packets a no-op (§4 step 2)', () async {
    const packet = "('v1', 'soc', TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 10:00:00', 55, now())";
    await db.read.execute('INSERT INTO signal_reading VALUES $packet');
    await db.read.execute(
      'INSERT INTO signal_reading VALUES $packet ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING',
    );

    expect(await rows('SELECT count(*) FROM signal_reading'), [
      [1],
    ]);
  });

      INSERT INTO vehicle_signal_latest AS l VALUES
        ('v1', 'soc', TIMESTAMP '$ts', $value)
      ON CONFLICT (vehicle_id, signal) DO UPDATE
        SET value = excluded.value, event_ts = excluded.event_ts
        WHERE excluded.event_ts > l.event_ts
    ''');

Three callers, one\n/// definition of what a trip is.\n///\n/// A trip is **not** its own observation. It is a reading of\n/// `geofence_transition`, which is itself a reading of `location_fix`. Nothing\n/// here looks at a position: if the detector is right about crossings, this is\n/// right about trips, and if it is wrong there is exactly one place to fix.\nlibrary;\n\nimport 'package:dart_duckdb/dart_duckdb.dart';\n\n/// Removes the trips this pass is about to rewrite.\n///\n/// The whole vehicle, not a suffix. `geofence_transition` holds a handful of\n/// rows per truck per day where `location_fix` holds thousands, so the\n/// incremental-resume machinery the detector needs (ARCHITECTURE.md \u00a77.1,\n/// `geofence_containment`) buys nothing here \u2014 and a full rebuild cannot\n/// disagree with itself at the seam.\n///\n/// ponytail: whole-vehicle rebuild every batch. If `geofence_transition` ever\n/// grows past a few thousand rows per vehicle, scope this to transitions at or\n/// after `staging_geo_scope.from_ts` and seed `inside_count` the way the\n/// detector seeds its zone.\nconst deleteScopedTrips = '''\nDELETE FROM trip t\nWHERE EXISTS (\n  SELECT 1 FROM staging_geo_scope s WHERE s.vehicle_id = t.vehicle_id\n)\n''';\n\n/// The derivation, as one query. Takes no parameters: a trip is a pure\n/// function of the crossings, the containment they fold up to, and the\n/// odometer log. There is no \"now\" in it, which is what makes re-running it\n/// after every batch a no-op when nothing moved.\n///\n/// * `crossing` \u2014 the scoped vehicles' crossings, with each fence's size.\n/// * `baseline` \u2014 how many fences the vehicle was inside **before its first\n///   recorded crossing**. Not zero: the detector establishes a zone on its\n///   first confirmation without emitting a transition (learning where a truck\n///   is is not watching it go there), so a truck that starts in the depot has\n///   an EXIT with no matching ENTRY. Recovered arithmetically as *inside now\n///   minus the net of every crossing since*, which needs no extra table.\n/// * `instant` \u2014 crossings collapsed per event time. Leaving a bay and the\n///   depot around it can land on the same fix, and a running sum that stepped\n///   through them one at a time would dip through a spurious zero.\n/// * `counted` / `marked` \u2014 the running containment count and its previous\n///   value. \u00a77.2's `inside_count`, seeded from `baseline`.\n/// * `boundary` \u2014 the count reaching **0** is a departure; leaving 0 is an\n///   arrival. Per-fence exits are never consulted, which is the whole reason\n///   a nested bay manufactures nothing.\n/// * `paired` \u2014 departures and arrivals strictly alternate, so the arrival\n///   that closes a departure is simply the next boundary row.\n///\n/// Among crossings sharing one instant, the fence named is the **largest**:\n/// a truck that leaves Bay 3 and Whitefield Depot on one fix departed from the\n/// depot. The same rule picks the outermost fence on arrival.\nconst tripDerivationQuery = '''\nWITH crossing AS (\n  SELECT t.vehicle_id, t.event_ts, t.kind, t.confidence,\n         t.geofence_id, g.radius_m\n  FROM geofence_transition t\n  JOIN staging_geo_scope s ON s.vehicle_id = t.vehicle_id\n  JOIN geofence g USING (geofence_id)\n),\nbaseline AS (\n  SELECT s.vehicle_id,\n         (SELECT count(*) FROM geofence_containment c\n           WHERE c.vehicle_id = s.vehicle_id AND c.zone = 'IN')\n         - coalesce((SELECT sum(CASE t.kind WHEN 'ENTRY' THEN 1 ELSE -1 END)\n                       FROM geofence_transition t\n                      WHERE t.vehicle_id = s.vehicle_id), 0) AS start_count\n  FROM staging_geo_scope s\n),\ninstant AS (\n  SELECT vehicle_id,\n         event_ts,\n         sum(CASE kind WHEN 'ENTRY' THEN 1 ELSE -1 END) AS delta,\n         arg_max(geofence_id, radius_m) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'EXIT')  AS exited,\n         arg_max(geofence_id, radius_m) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'ENTRY') AS entered,\n         bool_or(confidence = 'low') AS shaky\n  FROM crossing\n  GROUP BY vehicle_id, event_ts\n),\ncounted AS (\n  SELECT i.*,\n         b.start_count,\n         b.start_count + sum(i.delta) OVER (\n           PARTITION BY i.vehicle_id ORDER BY i.event_ts\n         ) AS inside_count\n  FROM instant i JOIN baseline b ON b.vehicle_id = i.vehicle_id\n),\nmarked AS (\n  SELECT *,\n         lag(inside_count) OVER (\n           PARTITION BY vehicle_id ORDER BY event_ts\n         ) AS prev_count\n  FROM counted\n),\nboundary AS (\n  SELECT vehicle_id, event_ts, exited, entered, shaky,\n         inside_count = 0 AS departing\n  FROM marked\n  WHERE (inside_count = 0 AND coalesce(prev_count, start_count) > 0)\n     OR (inside_count > 0 AND prev_count = 0)\n),\npaired AS (\n  SELECT *,\n         lead(event_ts) OVER w AS end_ts,\n         lead(entered)  OVER w AS dest,\n         lead(shaky)    OVER w AS end_shaky\n  FROM boundary\n  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY vehicle_id ORDER BY event_ts)\n),\nleg AS (SELECT * FROM paired WHERE departing),\nodo AS (\n  SELECT vehicle_id, event_ts, value\n  FROM signal_reading WHERE signal = 'odometer'\n)\n''';\n\n/// Writes the derived trips.\n///\n/// `trip_id` is derived from `(vehicle_id, start_ts)` rather than random, so a\n/// replay reproduces the identical row and a duplicate packet cannot fork a\n/// trip in two. /// Wall-clock access, injected rather than called statically.
///
/// Freshness, the OFFLINE rule and alert evaluation all compare event time

abstract class Clock {
  /// The current instant, in UTC. Always UTC: DuckDB `TIMESTAMP` columns carry
  /// no zone, so mixing local time in would make comparisons silently wrong.
  DateTime nowUtc();
}

/// The real clock, used everywhere outside tests.
class SystemClock implements Clock {
  const SystemClock();

  @override
  DateTime nowUtc() => DateTime.now().toUtc();
}

/// A clock the caller advances by hand, for deterministic tests.
class FakeClock implements Clock {
  FakeClock(this._now);

  DateTime _now;

  @override
  DateTime nowUtc() => _now;

  /// Moves the clock forward by [delta].
  void advance(Duration delta) => _now = _now.add(delta);

import 'package:byte_beam_project/db/fleet_db.dart';
import 'package:byte_beam_project/db/geofence_sql.dart';
import 'package:dart_duckdb/dart_duckdb.dart';
import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart';

import '../../duckdb_support.dart';

final t0 = DateTime.utc(2026, 1, 1, 8);

DateTime at(int minutes) => t0.add(Duration(minutes: minutes));

/// Fence centre used by every test: one fence, radius 1000 m, so the numbers
/// in the tests are metres from a single point.
const fenceLat = 12.9700;
const fenceLon = 77.6000;
const radius = 1000.0;

/// A latitude [metres] north of the fence centre. Longitude is left alone so
/// the offset is exactly the distance.
double latAt(double metres) => fenceLat + metres / 111320.0;

/// Entry and exit detection, driven through the real detector SQL.
void main() {
  setUpAll(useHostDuckDb);

  late FleetDb db;
  late Connection conn;

  setUp(() async {
    db = await FleetDb.open(':memory:');
    conn = db.read;
    await conn.execute('DELETE FROM geofence');
    await conn.execute("INSERT INTO vehicle VALUES ('v1', 'KA01AA0001', 'eT')");
    await conn.execute(
      "INSERT INTO geofence VALUES ('gf', 'Depot', $fenceLat, $fenceLon, "
      "$radius, TIMESTAMP '2000-01-01', NULL, TIMESTAMP '2000-01-01')",
    );
    await conn.execute(geofenceScopeDdl);
  });
  tearDown(() => db.close());

  /// Records one position fix [metres] from the fence centre.
  Future<void> fix(
    int minute,
    double metres, {
    double accuracy = 5,
    int second = 0,
    String vehicleId = 'v1',
  }) {
    final ts = at(minute).add(Duration(seconds: second));
    return conn.execute(
      "INSERT INTO location_fix VALUES ('$vehicleId', "
      "TIMESTAMP '${ts.toIso8601String()}', ${latAt(metres)}, "
      '$fenceLon, $accuracy, now())',
    );
  }

  /// Runs a derivation pass over everything, the way a fence edit does.
  Future<void> derive() => recomputeAllGeofences(conn);

  /// Every transition, oldest first.
  Future<List<List<Object?>>> transitions() async {
    final result = await conn.query(
      'SELECT kind, event_ts, confidence FROM geofence_transition '
      'ORDER BY event_ts',
    );
    return result.fetchAll();
  }

  Future<List<Object?>> containment() async {
    final result = await conn.query(
      'SELECT zone, pending_zone, pending_ts FROM geofence_containment',

  bucketed out of the event log.

  raise, escalate in place, resolve on observed recovery, dismiss with a
  reason, undo for five seconds. Alerts are episodes, not flags.

  fences; entry/exit detected in SQL from event-time position history with a
  hysteresis band, two-fix confirmation and a resumable containment state.

{
  "command": "cat > docs/06-trips.md <<'MD'\n# 06 \u2014 Automatic trips\n\nLegs between geofences, derived on every ingest batch from the crossings the\ndetector produces. Nothing in the packet stream says \"departed\".\n\nCovers the brief's \u00a73 E.\n\n## Files\n\n```\nlib/db/trip_sql.dart          the derivation, and the two read queries\nlib/features/trips/\n  domain/entities/            trip\n  domain/repositories/        trip_repository\n  domain/usecases/            get_recent_trips\n  data/models/                trip_model\n  data/datasources/           trip_local_data_source (interface + DuckDB impl)\n  data/repositories/          trip_repository_impl\n  presentation/               trips_controller \u00b7 trips_binding \u00b7 trips_page\n  presentation/widgets/       trip_tile\n```\n\nNo migration. `trip` has been in the schema since v1.\n\n## What a trip is\n\n**Containment count reaching zero.** Not a fence exit \u2014 a fence exit is what a\nnested bay produces every time a truck crosses its own yard, and keying off one\nwould turn a single departure into two trips.\n\n| Event | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| count falls to **0** | a trip starts; origin is the fence just left |\n| count rises **off 0** | the open trip completes; destination is the fence just entered |\n| still 0 at the end of the log | `IN_PROGRESS`. No timeout |\n| an arrival with no departure | nothing. We never watched it leave |\n\nOne open trip per vehicle falls out of the model rather than being enforced: a\ncount cannot be at zero twice without leaving zero in between. The real run\nbelow confirms it rather than the schema.\n\n## The derivation\n\nOne query, no parameters. A trip is a pure function of the crossings, the\ncontainment they fold up to, and the odometer log \u2014 there is no \"now\" in it,\nwhich is what makes re-running it after every batch a no-op when nothing moved.\n\n| Stage | What it does |\n|---|---|\n| `crossing` | the scoped vehicles' crossings, with each fence's size |\n| `baseline` | how many fences the vehicle was inside **before its first recorded crossing** |\n| `instant` | crossings collapsed per event time |\n| `counted` \u00b7 `marked` | the running count and its previous value |\n| `boundary` | count at 0 is a departure; leaving 0 is an arrival |\n| `paired` | the arrival closing a departure is the next boundary row |\n\nThree of those carry the design.\n\n**The baseline is not zero, and recovering it needs no table.** The detector\nemits no transition for the zone it establishes on a cold start \u2014 learning\nwhere a truck is is not watching it go there \u2014 so a truck that was already in\nthe depot has an EXIT with no matching ENTRY. Counting from zero would take it\nto \u22121 and lose the trip entirely. The count before the first crossing is\nrecovered arithmetically as *inside now, minus the net of every crossing\nsince*, which is exact and costs one scalar subquery.\n\n**Simultaneous crossings collapse into one instant.** Leaving Bay 3 and\nWhitefield Depot can be confirmed off the same fix. A running sum stepping\nthrough them one at a time would dip through a spurious zero and manufacture a\nzero-length trip, so the count only ever takes its post-instant value. Among\ncrossings sharing an instant the fence named is the **largest** \u2014 a truck that\nleaves the bay and the depot together departed from the depot, and the same\nrule picks the outermost fence on arrival.\n\n**Distance is an `ASOF LEFT JOIN` onto the odometer log** at each end: the last\nreading at or before that instant, and NULL when there is none. An open trip\nanchors its far end at `infinity`, so its distance is the distance *so far* and\ngrows with the truck. NULL rather than 0 when the odometer never reported \u2014\n\"we do not know\" and \"it did not move\" are different answers, and the UI says\n`distance unknown` rather than inventing the cheaper one.\n\n## Recompute, and what it costs\n\nWhole vehicle, every time, for every vehicle the batch touched. The detector\nneeds `geofence_containment` to resume mid-stream because `location_fix` holds\nthousands of rows per truck; `geofence_transition` holds a handful, so the\nsame machinery here would buy nothing and add a seam that can disagree with\nitself. Delete the vehicle's trips, rebuild from its whole crossing log.\n\nThat makes the hard cases somebody else's problem, which is the point:\n\n- **a duplicate packet** changes no crossing, so it changes no trip;\n- **a late packet** already forces the detector to replay that vehicle, and the\n  trips fall out of the replayed crossings;\n- **a fence edit** re-derives every crossing, and trips are re-derived right\n  after it in the same transaction.\n\n`trip_id` is `vehicle_id|epoch_ms(start_ts)` \u2014 derived, so a replay reproduces\nthe identical row. That is the backstop, not the mechanism.\n\nOrder matters, and it is pinned by a test rather than by a comment: detect,\nthen derive trips, then move the watermark. The baseline reads containment the\ndetector has just rewritten, and the detector reads the watermark to decide\nwhich vehicles went backwards.\n\n## What the real app produced\n\n40 vehicles, a few minutes of simulated driving, read straight out of the\ndatabase afterwards:\n\n```\n8655 location fixes \u00b7 18 crossings \u00b7 8 trips (5 running, 1 low confidence)\noverlapping trips per vehicle ........ 0\nopen trips followed by another ....... 0\nmax open trips on any one vehicle .... 1\n```\n\nCompleted legs included `Whitefield Depot \u2192 Whitefield Depot` and\n`Hebbal Yard \u2192 Hebbal Yard` \u2014 return-to-origin, which is an ordinary\ncompletion here and not a special case in the code.\n\nThe distances are honest and tiny (tens of metres). That is\n`SimulatorConfig.groundScale` showing through: the simulator moves vehicles\nacross the ground 30\u00d7 faster than their speed signal implies so that a geofence\ndemo produces crossings in a minute instead of twenty, and the odometer stays\nconsistent with the *honest* speed. Geography is scaled; the odometer is not.\nSet `groundScale` to 1 and the two agree again, at the cost of a demo nobody\ncan watch.\n\n## Tests\n\n| Claim | Test |\n|---|---|\n| leaving the last fence starts a running trip | `trip_derivation_test` |\n| arriving completes it; returning to origin is ordinary | `trip_derivation_test` |\n| an arrival with no departure makes nothing | `trip_derivation_test` |\n| leaving a bay inside a depot starts nothing | `trip_derivation_test`, `trip_store_test` |\n| bay + depot on one fix is one trip, from the depot | `trip_derivation_test` |\n| a cold start inside a fence still produces the trip | `trip_derivation_test` |\n| distance is the odometer delta, and NULL when absent | `trip_derivation_test` |\n| a running trip measures distance so far | `trip_derivation_test`, `trip_store_test` |\n| a low-confidence crossing makes a low-confidence trip | `trip_derivation_test` |\n| deriving twice changes nothing | `trip_derivation_test` |\n| a late fix moves the departure instead of adding a trip | `trip_store_test` |\n| one vehicle's list agrees with the fleet list | `trip_store_test` |\n| the screen says what would make a trip when there are none | `trip_page_test` |\n\n`trip_derivation_test` states crossing sequences directly and asks what they\nmean; `trip_store_test` drives a truck around through the real writer isolate\nand asks whether a trip comes out. The first would pass if the detector were\nbroken, the second would not, and neither would catch what the other does.\n\n## Knowingly left undone\n\n- **A fence deactivated while a vehicle is inside it holds that vehicle's count\n  above zero forever**, so the truck starts no further trips. Containment keeps\n  the last zone it was confirmed in and the fence stops producing opinions,\n  which is the same principle the alerts use \u2014 an episode ends when we watch it\n  end. Here the principle costs something real. Every alternative invents a\n  fact: an implicit exit at `active_to` manufactures a departure out of a\n  fence edit, and excluding deactivated fences retroactively deletes the trips\n  that named them. The fix, if it matters, is to purge containment rows on\n  deactivation and accept that the fence's live count goes to zero with them.\n  Recorded as ARCHITECTURE.md \u00a710, ambiguity 16.\n- **No trip route.** The fixes between the two ends are in `location_fix` and\n  nothing reads them. A route needs a map, which is the \u00a711 cut.\n- **No per-trip driver, load or purpose.** Nothing in the packet stream carries\n  them.\n- **The whole-vehicle rebuild is bounded by transition volume, not measured.**\n  It is a `ponytail:` comment on `deleteScopedTrips` with the upgrade path,\n  not a benchmark.\nMD\necho written"
}

```
No migration — `trip` has been in the schema since v1.

**A trip is the containment count reaching zero, not a fence exit.** A fence exit is what a nested bay produces every time a truck crosses its own yard; keying off one turns a single departure into two trips. Count falls to 0 → departure, origin is the fence just left. Count leaves 0 → arrival. Still 0 at the end → `IN_PROGRESS`, no timeout. One open trip per vehicle falls out of the model rather than being enforced.

Three parts carry weight:

- **The starting count is not zero, and recovering it needs no table.** The detector emits no transition for the zone it establishes on a cold start, so a truck already in the depot has an EXIT with no matching ENTRY — counting from zero takes it to −1 and loses the trip. The count before the first crossing is recovered as *inside now, minus the net of every crossing since*. Exact, one scalar subquery.
- **Simultaneous crossings collapse into one instant.** Leaving Bay 3 and the depot around it can be confirmed off the same fix; a sum stepping through them one at a time dips through a spurious zero. Among crossings sharing an instant the fence named is the largest — that truck departed from the depot, not the bay.
- **Distance is an `ASOF LEFT JOIN` onto the odometer at each end**, NULL when a reading is missing. An open trip anchors its far end at `infinity`, so it shows distance *so far*. The UI says `distance unknown` rather than 0.

**I did not build the incremental seed ARCHITECTURE.md promised, and that's the main deviation.** `geofence_transition` holds a handful of rows per truck where `location_fix` holds thousands, so the resume machinery that earns its place in the detector would buy nothing here and add a seam that can disagree with itself. Trips are deleted and rebuilt for the whole vehicle. That makes duplicates, late packets and fence edits need no handling at all — they're already handled one layer down, in the crossings. §7.2 and the doc both say so, with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and the upgrade path.

**Verified on the real app** (40 vehicles, 8655 fixes, 18 crossings → 8 trips, 5 running): 0 overlapping trips, 0 open trips followed by another, max 1 open trip per vehicle. Completed legs included `Whitefield Depot → Whitefield Depot` — return-to-origin, ordinary here, not a special case in the code.

One honest wart in that run: the distances are tens of metres. That's `groundScale` showing through — geography is scaled 30×, the odometer is not. Documented in the trips doc rather than tuned away.

**258 tests, analyzer clean, formatter clean.** Everything uncommitted.

skipped: no route line (needs a map — existing §11 cut), no driver/load/purpose (not in the packet stream). One real limitation recorded as ambiguity 16 rather than fixed: deactivating a fence while a truck is inside it pins that truck's count above zero, so it starts no further trips — every alternative invents a fact, and the fix is a containment purge on deactivation if it ever matters.

/// What one ingest batch actually did.
///
/// The counts are not cosmetic. `offered` minus `applied` is the duplicate
/// count, which is the visible proof that re-delivering a packet is a no-op —
/// the property the whole late/duplicate/out-of-order story rests on (§0).
class IngestReceipt {
  const IngestReceipt({
    required this.packets,
    required this.signalRowsOffered,
    required this.signalRowsApplied,
    required this.locationRowsOffered,
    required this.locationRowsApplied,
    required this.lateVehicles,
    required this.duration,
  });

  /// An empty receipt, for a batch that contained nothing.
  const IngestReceipt.empty()
    : packets = 0,
      signalRowsOffered = 0,
      signalRowsApplied = 0,
      locationRowsOffered = 0,
      locationRowsApplied = 0,
      lateVehicles = 0,
      duration = Duration.zero;

  /// How many packets were in the batch.
  final int packets;

  /// Signal rows the batch contained after de-duplicating within the batch.
  final int signalRowsOffered;

  /// Signal rows that were genuinely new. The rest collided with the natural
  /// key and were dropped by the database, not by application code.
  final int signalRowsApplied;

  final int locationRowsOffered;
  final int locationRowsApplied;

  /// Vehicles in this batch that reported an event time *behind* the position
  /// derivation had already reached. These are the ones whose geofence
  /// transitions and trips will need replaying once derivation exists (§4
  /// step 4). Counted now so the number is visible from the first commit.
  final int lateVehicles;

  /// Wall-clock time the batch took, measured in the writer isolate.
  final Duration duration;

  /// Rows rejected as duplicates — the difference between what was offered
  /// and what the database accepted.
  int get duplicateRows =>
      (signalRowsOffered - signalRowsApplied) +
      (locationRowsOffered - locationRowsApplied);

  @override
  String toString() =>
      'IngestReceipt($packets packets, '
      '${signalRowsApplied + locationRowsApplied} applied, '
      '$duplicateRows duplicates, $lateVehicles late, ${duration.inMilliseconds}ms)';
}

    }

  /// Count per status, plus the total for the "All" chip.
  Future<Map<FleetFilter, int>> _counts(DateTime now) async {
    final result = await _query(
      '$scoredCte SELECT status, count(*) FROM scored GROUP BY status',
      now,
    );

    final counts = {for (final filter in FleetFilter.values) filter: 0};
    var total = 0;
    for (final row in result.fetchAll()) {
      final status = VehicleStatus.fromSql(row[0]! as String);
      final count = (row[1]! as num).toInt();
      total += count;
      counts[_filterFor(status)] = count;
    }
    counts[FleetFilter.all] = total;
    return counts;
  }

  /// The rows for one chip, ordered by registration so the list is stable
  /// between refreshes — an order that jumps as speeds change is unreadable.
  Future<List<FleetVehicleSummaryModel>> _vehicles(
    FleetFilter filter,
    DateTime now,
  ) async {
    final status = filter.status;
    final where = status == null ? '' : "WHERE status = '${status.sqlName}'";
    final result = await _query(
      '$scoredCte SELECT vehicle_id, reg_no, model, status, soc, range_km, '
      'speed, last_ping, alert_severity FROM scored $where ORDER BY reg_no',
      now,
    );
    return [
      for (final row in result.fetchAll())
        FleetVehicleSummaryModel.fromRow(row),
    ];
  }

  /// Runs a statement built on [scoredCte], binding the instant to compare
  /// freshness against.
  ///
  /// `now` is bound rather than taken from SQL's own `now()` so tests can pin
  /// it — a fleet list whose rules depend on the wall clock is untestable.
  Future<ResultSet> _query(String sql, DateTime now) async {
    final statement = await _read.prepare(sql);
    try {
      statement.bindParams([now]);
      return await statement.execute();
    } finally {
      await statement.dispose();
    }
  }

{
  "command": "cat > lib/db/backfill_sql.dart <<'DART'\n/// The scale exercise's backfill: 500 vehicles and a couple of million signal\n/// rows, generated **inside DuckDB**.\n///\n/// Generating the rows in Dart and pushing them across the FFI boundary would\n/// take minutes; `range()` cross-joined against itself takes seconds, because\n/// nothing ever leaves the engine. That is the whole technique \u2014 the SQL below\n/// is one statement per table.\n///\n/// Values are deterministic rather than `random()`. Two reasons: re-running\n/// the backfill then inserts nothing (the natural key rejects every row), and\n/// a fleet list full of plausible numbers is a demo while one full of noise is\n/// a screenshot of a bug report.\nlibrary;\n\nimport 'package:dart_duckdb/dart_duckdb.dart';\n\nimport 'alert_sql.dart';\nimport 'geofence_sql.dart';\nimport 'trip_sql.dart';\n\n/// Signals generated, with the range each one moves through.\n///\n/// The six from `signal_spec`, because the register, the verdict pills and the\n/// alert evaluator all read that table and a backfill that skipped one would\n/// leave a permanent \"\u2014\" on every vehicle detail screen.\nconst _signals = \"(VALUES ('soc'), ('range_km'), ('speed'), \"\n    \"('battery_temp'), ('odometer'), ('ignition')) AS s(signal)\";\n\n/// Per-signal value, as a function of vehicle index and tick.\n///\n/// `sin` of a stride that is coprime with the tick count gives each vehicle\n/// its own slow wander rather than 500 copies of one curve. The odometer is\n/// monotone in *time* (`ticks - t.i`, since tick 0 is the newest), because an\n/// odometer that goes backwards makes every trip distance negative.\nconst _value = '''\nCASE s.signal\n  WHEN 'odometer'     THEN round(80000 + v.i * 137 + (\\$ticks - t.i) * 1.7, 1)\n  WHEN 'ignition'     THEN CASE WHEN (v.i + t.i) % 11 = 0 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END\n  WHEN 'soc'          THEN round(12 + 76 * abs(sin((v.i * 7 + t.i) / 53.0)), 1)\n  WHEN 'range_km'     THEN round(35 + 380 * abs(sin((v.i * 7 + t.i) / 53.0)), 1)\n  WHEN 'speed'        THEN round(78 * abs(sin((v.i * 3 + t.i) / 17.0)), 1)\n  ELSE                     round(21 + 27 * abs(sin((v.i + t.i) / 29.0)), 1)\nEND''';\n\n/// Backfills [vehicles] trucks with [ticks] reports each, ending at [now].\n///\n/// Returns row counts and the wall-clock split between loading the log and\n/// re-deriving everything on top of it \u2014 the second number is the interesting\n/// one, and the one a reader would otherwise assume was zero.\n///\n/// Runs in the caller's transaction. The caller is the writer isolate, which\n/// is the only thing allowed to write at all.\nFuture<Map<String, int>> backfillFleet(\n  Connection conn, {\n  required DateTime now,\n  int vehicles = 500,\n  int ticks = 700,\n  Duration span = const Duration(days: 7),\n}) async {\n  final step = span.inSeconds ~/ ticks;\n  final loading = Stopwatch()..start();\n\n  // Registration plates are the backfill's own series so a backfilled fleet is\n  // distinguishable from a simulated one at a glance, and so the two can share\n  // a database without colliding.\n  await conn.execute('''\n    INSERT INTO vehicle\n    SELECT 'bf-' || i, 'KA99BF' || lpad(CAST(i AS TEXT), 4, '0'), 'eT 1000'\n    FROM range(0, $vehicles) r(i)\n    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING\n  ''');\n\n  await conn.execute('''\n    INSERT INTO signal_reading\n    SELECT 'bf-' || v.i,\n           s.signal,\n           CAST(\\$now AS TIMESTAMP) - to_seconds(t.i * $step),\n           ${_value.replaceAll(r'$ticks', '$ticks')},\n           CAST(now() AS TIMESTAMP)\n    FROM range(0, $vehicles) v(i)\n    CROSS JOIN $_signals\n    CROSS JOIN range(0, $ticks) t(i)\n    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING\n  '''.replaceAll(r'$now', \"TIMESTAMP '${now.toIso8601String()}'\"));\n\n  // One position per report, the way the simulator emits them.   required DateTime now,

}) async {
  final horizon = "TIMESTAMP '${now.subtract(keep).toIso8601String()}'";
  final before = await _databaseBytes(conn);

  // Summarise and drop in one transaction: a crash between them would leave
  // buckets duplicating rows that are still live. The CHECKPOINT afterwards is
  // outside it, because it cannot run inside a transaction — and it is the
  // step that actually returns the pages rather than parking them in the WAL.

  final int fixes;

    await conn.execute('''

      SELECT vehicle_id,
             signal,
             time_bucket(INTERVAL '${width.inSeconds} seconds', event_ts),
             count(*),
             min(value),
             max(value),
             avg(value),
             arg_max(value, event_ts)
      FROM signal_reading
      WHERE event_ts < $horizon
      GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
      ON CONFLICT (vehicle_id, signal, bucket_ts) DO UPDATE

            max_value = excluded.max_value,
            avg_value = excluded.avg_value,

    fixes = await _countOf(

      'DELETE FROM location_fix WHERE event_ts < $horizon',
    );
    await conn.execute('COMMIT');
  } catch (_) {
    await conn.execute('ROLLBACK');
    rethrow;
  }

  await conn.execute('CHECKPOINT');

import 'package:get/get.dart';

import '../../../../core/db/database_pulse.dart';
import '../../../../core/utils/clock.dart';
import '../../../../db/fleet_db.dart';
import '../../data/datasources/simulated_packet_source.dart';
import '../../data/datasources/simulator_config.dart';
import '../../data/datasources/telemetry_local_data_source.dart';
import '../../data/datasources/telemetry_packet_source.dart';
import '../../data/datasources/telemetry_writer_isolate.dart';
import '../../data/repositories/telemetry_repository_impl.dart';
import '../../domain/repositories/telemetry_repository.dart';
import '../../domain/usecases/get_ingest_snapshot.dart';
import '../../domain/usecases/ingest_packet_batch.dart';
import '../../domain/usecases/observe_telemetry.dart';
import '../../domain/usecases/seed_fleet.dart';
import '../controllers/ingest_controller.dart';

/// Wires the feature together.
///
/// This is the only place the concrete classes are named. Everything else asks
/// for an interface, which is what makes the dependency arrows in this feature
/// point inwards: presentation to domain, data to domain, never the reverse.
///
/// Registered eagerly rather than lazily because spawning the writer isolate
/// is async and the screen must not build before it is ready.
class IngestBinding extends Bindings {
  IngestBinding({
    required this.db,
    this.config = const SimulatorConfig(),
    this.clock = const SystemClock(),
  });

  final FleetDb db;
  final SimulatorConfig config;
  final Clock clock;

  /// Builds and registers the object graph.
  ///
  /// Async because the writer isolate has to be up before the controller can
  /// write anything; call it and await it before navigating to the page.
  Future<void> dependenciesAsync() async {
    final local = await DuckDbTelemetryLocalDataSource.create(db);
    final source = SimulatedPacketSource(clock: clock, config: config);

    Get.put<TelemetryLocalDataSource>(local, permanent: true);
    // The single writer, registered on its own so the alerts feature can send
    // dismissals through it without going via this feature's repository.
    Get.put<TelemetryWriter>(local.writer, permanent: true);
    Get.put<TelemetryPacketSource>(source, permanent: true);
    Get.put<TelemetryRepository>(
      TelemetryRepositoryImpl(local: local, source: source, clock: clock),
      permanent: true,
    );

    final repository = Get.find<TelemetryRepository>();
    final controller = Get.put(
      IngestController(
        seedFleet: SeedFleet(repository),
        observeTelemetry: ObserveTelemetry(repository),
        ingestPacketBatch: IngestPacketBatch(repository),
        getIngestSnapshot: GetIngestSnapshot(repository),
        roster: source.fleet,
        pulse: Get.find<DatabasePulse>(),
      ),
      permanent: true,
    );

    // Start the pipeline here rather than relying on a lifecycle hook: the
    // feed must run even though its monitor screen is not the home screen.
    await controller.bootstrap();
  }

  /// GetX's synchronous hook. The graph is built in [dependenciesAsync] before
  /// the route is pushed, so there is nothing left to do here.
  @override
  void dependencies() {}
}

Each one stops the telemetry feed first, because a measurement taken\nwhile something else is writing measures both.\n\nThe same three run headless, which is how every number below was taken:\n\n```bash\nflutter run -d macos --release --dart-define=SCALE_BACKFILL=true\nflutter run -d macos --release --dart-define=SCALE_BENCH=true\nflutter run -d macos --release --dart-define=SCALE_COMPACT=true --dart-define=SCALE_KEEP_MINUTES=60\n```\n\nThey print to stdout as `[scale] \u2026`. Compile-time constants, so a build\nwithout the defines contains none of it.\n\n## The backfill\n\nOne `INSERT \u2026 SELECT` per table, `range()` cross-joined against itself. Nothing\nleaves the engine \u2014 generating 2.17 M rows in Dart and pushing them across the\nFFI boundary would take minutes.\n\nValues are deterministic rather than `random()`, which buys two things: the\nbutton is safe to press twice (every row collides with the natural key the\nsecond time), and the fleet list fills with plausible numbers instead of noise.\nThe odometer is monotone in time, because a backwards odometer makes every trip\ndistance negative.\n\nReports land at a **10-second cadence**, so 700 reports per vehicle is about\ntwo hours of dense history rather than two weeks of one reading every half\nhour. A bulk load leaves every class D table\ndescribing a fleet that no longer exists, so the backfill finishes by running\nthe same derivations ingest runs \u2014 latest values, alerts, geofences, trips,\nwatermark \u2014 over the whole log. \u00a73.5 claims derived state is droppable and\nrebuildable; this is that claim executed.\n\n## The device\n\n| | |\n|---|---|\n| Machine | MacBook Pro (MacBookPro18,3), Apple M1 Pro, 16 GB |\n| OS | macOS 26.6.2 (25G83) |\n| Build | Flutter 3.35.6, `flutter run -d macos --release` |\n| Database | 540 vehicles \u00b7 2 168 764 signal rows \u00b7 361 416 location fixes |\n\n**This is a desktop, and that matters.** An M1 Pro with 16 GB flatters every\nnumber here \u2014 a mid-range Android phone has a fraction of the memory bandwidth\nand a much smaller page cache. The project has no `ios/` directory and this\nmachine has no Android AVD, so macOS was the only target that could run the\nreal app; that is a limitation of the measurement, not a result. The numbers to\ntreat as load-bearing are the *ratios* and the diagnosis, not the absolutes.\n\n## The numbers\n\n### Cold start \u2192 first painted fleet list\n\n`main()` starts a `Stopwatch`; the fleet page registers a one-shot\n`addTimingsCallback` on the first build that has vehicles, and stops the clock\nwhen that frame is rasterised. \"With data\" matters \u2014 stopping on the first\nframe would measure the spinner.\n\n| Launch | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| ms | 1318 | 1287 | 1433 | 1461 |\n\n**\u22481.3\u20131.5 s against a 2.17 M-row database. Target was 2.5 s.** The spread is\nlaunch-to-launch page-cache variation, not load.\n\n### Fleet-list query, warm\n\n100 runs of **both** statements one refresh issues \u2014 the chip counts and the\nrows \u2014 timed inside the writer isolate, rows fetched rather than merely\nplanned, after three untimed warm-up passes. All 100 samples are in\n[`docs/data/fleet-query-bench-macos.csv`](data/fleet-query-bench-macos.csv); a\np95 with no distribution behind it is a number nobody can argue with.\n\n| p50 | p95 | p99 | min | max |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 10.06 ms | 12.48 ms | 15.75 ms | 8.51 ms | 20.27 ms |\n\n**p95 12.5 ms against a target of 25 ms.** The query never touches the\n2.17 M-row log: it reads `vehicle_signal_latest`, which is 3 240 rows. That is\nthe entire reason the number is flat \u2014 the latest-value table exists so the\nfleet list's cost is a function of fleet size rather than of history.\n\nTimed in the writer isolate on purpose. A query timed on the UI isolate between\ntwo builds measures the frame scheduler as well.\n\n### Memory at rest, list open\n\n`footprint -p <pid>`, taken 90 seconds after launch with the fleet list open\nand the simulator feed running \u2014 the app's actual resting state, not an idle\none.\n\n| | |\n|---|---|\n| Settled | **234 MB** |\n| Peak during launch | 383 MB |\n| Peak during the backfill | 881 MB |\n\n**Under the 250 MB target, but not comfortably.** `footprint` puts 150 MB of\nit in `MALLOC_SMALL` with another 247 MB reclaimable \u2014 DuckDB's buffer pool and\nthe ART index on `signal_reading`'s three-column primary key, which is exactly\nwhere \u00a78 predicted it would be.\n\nIf this had to come down, the fix is the one already written down: drop the\nprimary key and dedupe with an ANTI JOIN against a bounded recent window.\nDuplicates only ever arrive near the present, so an index over all of history\nearns nothing. It is not done here because 234 MB is inside budget on this\nmachine and the change trades a database-enforced invariant \u2014 \u00a70's whole\nfoundation \u2014 for memory that is not yet short.\n\nThe 881 MB backfill peak is a debug action loading 2.5 M rows in one\ntransaction, not a state the app reaches in use.\n\n## Two things that were measured and were wrong\n\n**The load-then-index trick could not be applied, and it is worth 4\u00d7.**\nARCHITECTURE.md \u00a78 promised the table would be bulk-loaded without its primary\nkey and indexed once afterwards. Measured, on this machine, for the same\n2.1 M rows:\n\n| Method | Time |\n|---|---|\n| `INSERT` into a table that already has the PK | 2467 ms |\n| `INSERT` into a plain table, then `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` | 606 ms (230 + 376) |\n\nFour times faster, and the backfill does **not** do it: `signal_reading` is\ncreated with its primary key in migration v1, and DuckDB 1.2.1 answers\n`ALTER TABLE \u2026 DROP CONSTRAINT` with *\"No support for that ALTER TABLE option\nyet\"*. Applying the trick would mean forking the schema for a debug action. The\nbackfill pays 4288 ms instead, which is a one-off button press.\n\n**The first retention implementation made the database bigger.** It rolled\nevery old reading into a five-minute bucket and dropped the raw rows \u2014 and on\nthe first backfill, whose reports were 29 minutes apart, every bucket held\nexactly one reading. 1 050 000 readings became 1 050 000 buckets, each carrying\nfour more columns than the row it replaced, and the file grew from 148 MiB to\n274.5 MiB. The fix is a `HAVING count(*) > 1`: a reading alone in its bucket is\nalready at the policy's resolution, so it stays where it is. There is a test\nfor it now.\n\n## Retention policy\n\n**`signal_reading` keeps 7 days at full resolution.** Everything older is\nsummarised per `(vehicle, signal)` into 5-minute buckets \u2014 count, min, max,\naverage and last \u2014 and the raw rows are dropped, followed by a `CHECKPOINT`.\nmin and max as well as average, because an average hides exactly the thing\nanyone looks at old battery data for: how hot did it actually get.\n\n**`location_fix` is dropped on the same horizon and not summarised.** The\naverage of two positions is not a position.\n\n**Derived tables \u2014 transitions, trips, alerts, rollups \u2014 are kept\nindefinitely.** They are small, and they are the only record of what the\ndropped rows meant.\n\nMeasured on the real database. The demo holds about two hours of history, so\nthis run used a 60-minute window rather than 7 days; the policy is unchanged,\nthe window is a `--dart-define`:\n\n| | |\n|---|---|\n| Readings dropped | 1 110 004 |\n| Buckets written | 39 240 (**28:1**) |\n| Position fixes dropped | 184 975 |\n| Bytes in use | 185.8 MiB \u2192 **135.5 MiB** |\n| File size | 260.0 MiB \u2192 260.0 MiB |\n\nThe file does not shrink, and that is not a bug: DuckDB reuses freed blocks\nrather than returning them to the operating system. *Bytes in use* is the\nnumber that moves, which is why the screen reports both \u2014 showing only the file\nsize would make a working policy look broken.\n\n### What the app loses\n\n- **The sub-5-minute shape of old data.** A battery spike that lasted 90\n  seconds nine days ago survives as that bucket's `max_value` and nothing else.\n- **The ability to re-derive geofence transitions or trips outside the hot\n  window.** A crossing needs individual fixes; the average of a latitude is not\n  a position. This is why \u00a710's ambiguity 5 rejects a packet older than the\n  window and counts it, rather than applying it \u2014 applying it would produce\n  derived state that no longer follows from the log.\n- **Nothing already derived.** Trips and transitions from before the horizon\n  are kept; only the ability to *recompute* them goes.\n\n## Tests\n\n| Claim | Test |\n|---|---|\n| six signals per vehicle per tick, all known to `signal_spec` | `backfill_test` |\n| running the backfill twice inserts nothing | `backfill_test` |\n| the odometer only ever increases | `backfill_test` |\n| latest values, containment and the watermark are rebuilt from the log | `backfill_test` |\n| the fleet query answers for every backfilled vehicle | `backfill_test` |\n| readings inside the hot window are untouched | `retention_test` |\n| older readings are summarised, then dropped | `retention_test` |\n| a reading alone in its bucket is left where it is | `retention_test` |\n| min and max survive the average | `retention_test` |\n| position fixes are dropped, never summarised | `retention_test` |\n| compacting twice finds nothing left to do | `retention_test` |\n\n20 vehicles rather than 500 in the tests: the properties asserted are the same\nat both sizes, and the numbers that only matter at 500 are measurements, which\nbelong in this document with the device they came from.\n\n## Knowingly left undone\n\n- **No phone or emulator measurement.** The project has no `ios/` directory and\n  this machine has no Android AVD. Every number here is desktop, said plainly\n  above rather than buried.\n- **Compaction is manual.** A real build schedules it \u2014 on launch when the\n  oldest row is past the horizon, or on a periodic task. The policy and the\n  code are here; the trigger is a button.\n- **No rollup reader.** `signal_rollup` is written and never read. The SOC\n  history chart still queries `signal_reading` only, so a 30-day chart would\n  show 7 days and stop. Reading both and stitching them is the obvious next\n  step and is not done.\n- **`vehicle_signal_latest` is why the query is fast, and it is not stressed.**\n  A fleet of 50 000 vehicles would put 300 000 rows in it and this benchmark\n  says nothing about that.\nMD\necho ok"

lib/core/utils/cold_start.dart    the stopwatch
lib/features/scale/               scale_controller · scale_page
docs/07-scale.md · docs/data/fleet-query-bench-macos.csv
```

**Debug action:** Ingest monitor → Scale exercise, three buttons. Each stops the feed first. The same three run headless via `--dart-define=SCALE_BACKFILL/BENCH/COMPACT`, which is how every number below was taken.

**Device: MacBook Pro (M1 Pro, 16 GB, macOS 26.6.2), release build, 540 vehicles / 2 168 764 signal rows / 361 416 fixes.** This is a desktop and I say so in the doc — no `ios/` directory in the project, no Android AVD on the machine, so there is no phone number and I don't pretend otherwise.

| | Measured | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Cold start → first painted fleet list | 1318 / 1287 / 1433 / 1461 ms | < 2500 ms |
| Fleet query warm, 100 runs | p50 **10.06** · p95 **12.48** · p99 15.75 ms | p95 < 25 ms |
| Memory at rest, list open | **234 MB** (peak 383 at launch) | < 250 MB |

The query is flat because it never touches the log — it reads `vehicle_signal_latest`, 3 240 rows. All 100 samples are committed as CSV; a p95 with no distribution behind it is a number nobody can argue with.

**Two things I promised in ARCHITECTURE.md that turned out wrong, both now measured rather than quietly dropped:**

- **The load-then-index trick is worth 4× and cannot be applied.** 606 ms (230 load + 376 index) against 2467 ms for the same 2.1 M rows. But `signal_reading` gets its PK in migration v1, and DuckDB 1.2.1 answers `ALTER TABLE … DROP CONSTRAINT` with *"No support for that ALTER TABLE option yet"*. Forking the schema for a debug action isn't worth 3.7 s, so the backfill pays 4288 ms.
- **My first retention implementation made the database 126 MiB bigger.** It rolled up every old reading, and on a log sparser than the bucket every bucket held exactly one — 1 050 000 readings became 1 050 000 wider rows. Fixed with `HAVING count(*) > 1`; there's a test for it.

**Retention, executed:** 7 days raw, older readings → 5-minute min/max/avg/last buckets, raw dropped, `CHECKPOINT`; positions dropped, never averaged. On the real database (60-minute window, since the demo holds ~2 h): **1 110 004 readings → 39 240 buckets, 28:1**; bytes in use 185.8 → 135.5 MiB. The *file* stays 260 MiB because DuckDB never returns blocks to the OS, so the screen reports both — showing only file size would make a working policy look broken. What's lost: sub-bucket shape, and the ability to re-derive crossings or trips outside the window.

**Memory diagnosis:** 150 MB dirty in `MALLOC_SMALL` plus 247 MB reclaimable — the ART index on the three-column PK, exactly where §8 predicted. Inside budget, so I did not trade a database-enforced invariant for memory that isn't short yet; the ANTI-JOIN-on-a-recent-window fix is written down.

**272 tests, analyzer clean, formatter clean.** Everything uncommitted.

skipped: compaction is manual (button, not scheduler); `signal_rollup` is written but nothing reads it yet, so a 30-day chart still stops at 7 days.

BYTEBEAM HIRING
Page 1
Flutter Take-Home \227 Fleet Console\(Local-First\)
Role: Flutter Engineer \(SDE-3\), Bytebeam Expected effort: 14\22616 hours across a week. We do not time you. Asmaller scope done well beats everything done thinly \227 if you cut, say what you cut and why. Tools: Use AIassistants freely. We build with them daily. Two conditions follow: you share your conversation logs, and youdefend every decisions in a live session. Code you cannot explain counts against you more than code you did notwrite.
The difficulty is not volume of features \227 it is that the data model has genuinely ambiguous cases, and we want tosee how you resolve them.
1. Context
A fleet operator with 500 electric trucks needs one screen answering: where are my vehicles, are they okay, whatneeds attention now.
Vehicles emit telemetry \227 small sensor packets over a flaky mobile link. Packets arrive late, out of order,duplicated, or not at all. Vehicles park in basements for hours and then dump a backlog.
Glossary. SOC \227 battery state of charge, %. Range \227 estimated km remaining. Odometer \227 lifetime km. Ignition\227 vehicle switched on. Signal \227 one named telemetry parameter \(soc, speed, battery_temp, \205\). Packet \227 onetimestamped emission from one vehicle, carrying a subset of signals. Stale \227 last report too old to trust.
2. Architecture requirement \227 local-first over DuckDB
The app is local-first. Telemetry is written to an embedded DuckDB database on device \(dart_duckdb, currently^1.2.0 \227 ships its own binaries, works on Android\). The UI reads from DuckDB. The dismissal is written to DuckDB immediately and UNDO clears `dismissed_at`. It is not held in memory for 5 seconds \u2014 local-first means the database is the truth, and if the app dies mid-window the dismissal stands. That is the honest trade; the alternative loses a user's explicit action to a crash.\n\n**Resolution is independent.** The evaluator clears an alert when its condition clears, dismissed or not. A dismissed alert whose condition never clears simply stays hidden until the condition clears and re-triggers \u2014 dismissal suppresses the *episode*, not the *rule*.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Geofences and trips\n\n### 6.1 Transition detection\n\nDeterministic pipeline, applied per `(vehicle, geofence)` over event-time-ordered fixes:\n\n1. **Accuracy gate** \u2014 discard fixes with `accuracy_m > 100`. Filtered at read; nothing is ever deleted from the log.\n2. **Hysteresis** \u2014 inside if `d \u2264 r \u2212 h`, outside if `d \u2265 r + h`, with `h = max(25 m, accuracy_m)`. Fixes in the band produce **no zone opinion**.\n3. **Carry forward** \u2014 `last_value(zone IGNORE NULLS) OVER (PARTITION BY vehicle_id, geofence_id ORDER BY event_ts)`. The band is now genuinely inert rather than a source of flapping.\n4. **Confirm** \u2014 a crossing is confirmed when two consecutive opinionated fixes agree on the new zone. Escape hatch for a fast exit: one fix more than `2h` past the boundary confirms alone.\n5. **Timestamp** \u2014 the transition is stamped with the **first** fix of the confirming pair. Nothing is synthesised across a gap.\n7. **Overlaps** \u2014 no single \"current geofence\" internally; containment is per fence. The UI's single-value *current geofence* is the **smallest radius containing the vehicle**, tie-broken by `geofence_id`.\n8. **Fence activation** is time-versioned via `active_from` / `active_to`, so evaluation asks \"was this fence active at the fix's event time\" and recompute stays pure. **Geometry is not versioned** \u2014 editing centre or radius triggers a full recompute of that fence's transitions and the affected trips. Scale\n\n**Backfill.** 500 vehicles \u00d7 6 signals \u00d7 ~700 ticks \u2248 2.1 M rows, generated **inside DuckDB** with `range()` and `random()` in a single `INSERT \u2026 SELECT`. The table is created without the primary key, bulk-loaded, then `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` once \u2014 building the ART index in one pass instead of 2 M times.\n\n**Measurements to report**, on a named physical device plus a named emulator:\n\n| Metric | How | Target |\n|---|---|---|\n| Cold start \u2192 first painted fleet list | stopwatch from `main()`, stopped in `addTimingsCallback` on first frame with data | < 2.5 s |\n| Fleet-list query p50 / p95, warm | 100 runs in the writer isolate, dumped to CSV | p95 < 25 ms |\n| Memory at rest, list open | `adb shell dumpsys meminfo` PSS, DevTools cross-check | < 250 MB |\n\nIf a number is bad it gets reported as bad, with a diagnosis. Tests\n\nThe suite is built around the invariant from \u00a70, not around line coverage.\n\n**The test that matters:** generate a packet stream, shuffle it, inject duplicates and delays, replay it, and assert the derived state \u2014 latest values, alerts, transitions, trips \u2014 is identical to the in-order replay. Ambiguities and how they are resolved\n\nThe brief says the data model has genuinely ambiguous cases. These are the ones I found and the calls I made.\n\n| # | Ambiguity | Resolution | Rejected alternative |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Vehicle is online (odometer 2 min old) but `speed` is 40 min old. MOVING? | Status only reads **fresh** signals; a stale speed cannot claim MOVING or IDLE, so it falls through to STOPPED. STOPPED is the documented fallback bucket. | A sixth `UNKNOWN` chip \u2014 the brief specifies five. |\n| 2 | What is \"last ping\"? | `max(event_ts)` across all signals *and* location fixes for the vehicle. | Per-signal freshness only \u2014 the brief says vehicle-level. |\n| 3 | Event time or arrival time? | **Event time** drives every rule: freshness, status, alerts, transitions, trips. `ingest_ts` is audit only. | Arrival time \u2014 makes a backlog dump look like a fleet that just woke up. |\n| 4 | What is a duplicate? | Identity is `(vehicle_id, signal, event_ts)`. Same key, different value \u2192 keep the first, increment a conflict counter surfaced in a debug view. | Last-write-wins \u2014 non-deterministic under reordering, which breaks \u00a70. |\n| 5 | Packet older than the retention window | Rejected and counted. Scope cuts\n\nStated up front, per the brief.\n\n- **No backend, no auth, no sync.** The packet source is a simulator behind a one-method interface; a real MQTT/HTTP feed is a constructor swap.\n- **No map tiles in v1.** Geofences are created and edited by name / lat / lon / radius with a schematic canvas preview. `flutter_map` goes in only if time remains after tests \u2014 it is presentation, and every ambiguity above is decided without it.\n- **No background ingest while the app is killed.** No foreground service, no WorkManager.\n- **No severity/escalation audit trail.** The alert row carries `escalated_at`; the full state-change log is a table I would add the moment anyone asked \"why did this fire\".\n- **No i18n, no custom theme.** Material 3 defaults.\n\n---\n\n## 11. ### Claude — 2026-09-12T06:55:37.232Z
Read the PDF (had to un-ASCII85 it — no poppler on this box). Design written.

**[ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md)** — 11 sections. The spine:

**One idea:** derived state is a pure fold over the append-only log. Late/duplicate/reordered packets are handled by replaying the affected suffix, never by patching. Alerts, transitions and trips all fall out of that, and it gives you the one test worth writing: *shuffle the stream, inject duplicates, assert the final state equals in-order replay.*

**Concrete calls:**
- `signal_reading` PK `(vehicle, signal, event_ts)` → dedupe is a DB constraint, not a code path. Location gets its own table, not two paired signals.
- `vehicle_signal_latest` (~3k rows) is the entire read path — fleet list + chip counts are one SQL query over it, with a conditional `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE … WHERE excluded.event_ts > l.event_ts` so late packets can't clobber.
- Derivation in SQL window functions (`last_value … IGNORE NULLS`, `lag`, ASOF join), not a Dart fold — a Dart fold *is* the in-memory shadow the brief forbids.
- Jitter: 25 m hysteresis band + two-fix confirmation; band fixes carry the previous zone forward. Trips key off **containment count hitting 0**, not per-fence exits — so leaving a bay inside a depot starts nothing, and "one active trip" is free.
- Backfill generates 2.1 M rows *inside* DuckDB via `range()`, index built after load.

**§9 is the section they're actually grading** — 13 ambiguities in a table with the call and the rejected alternative (stale speed → STOPPED; stale signal does *not* resolve an alert; escalation un-dismisses; geometry not versioned but activation is; late packet past retention rejected and counted).

Also added **[tool/export_ai_logs.sh](tool/export_ai_logs.sh)** — dumps Claude session jsonl → `ai-logs/*.md`, uncurated, tool calls included. Smoke-tested against a real transcript dir (34 turns out clean). Run it from the project root or the slug won't match.

The design question is **who owns the truth for each row**, because that one classification decides the sync direction, the conflict rule, the transaction boundary, and whether the table can simply be thrown away and rebuilt. Every table in \u00a72 belongs to exactly one of three classes.\n\n| Class | Tables | Origin | Sync | Conflict | On migration / loss |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **R** \u2014 remote-authoritative, immutable | `vehicle`, `signal_reading`, `location_fix` | the trucks | pull, cursored | impossible by construction | re-pullable |\n| **L** \u2014 device-authored intent | `geofence`, `alert.dismissed_at`/`dismiss_reason` | the operator, on this device | push, via outbox | per-table rule, never a blanket policy | **the only data that can actually be lost** |\n| **D** \u2014 derived | `vehicle_signal_latest`, `geofence_transition`, `trip`, alert raise/resolve state | this device, from R + L | never synced | n/a | dropped and rebuilt |\n\n### 3.1 Class R \u2014 append-only, natural key, cursored pull\n\nRows are immutable and identified by a natural key (`(vehicle_id, signal, event_ts)`, `(vehicle_id, event_ts)`), written with `INSERT \u2026 ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, and the pull cursor advances **in the same transaction as the rows it covers**.\n\nThat combination buys the property offline-first actually needs: **at-least-once delivery is sufficient, because the write is idempotent.** No exactly-once protocol, no ack dance. Crash between fetch and commit? Re-pull the page; the constraint absorbs it. Dedupe is the *side effect* of the natural key, not its purpose.\n\nClass R is never row-updated. DuckDB is an OLAP engine \u2014 a per-row `UPDATE` or `DELETE` against a 2 M-row table is a rewrite, not an in-place poke. Confining all mutation to tables of a few thousand rows (`vehicle_signal_latest`, `alert`, `geofence`, per-vehicle slices of the derived tables) is not incidental tidiness; it is the reason the schema is shaped this way.\n\n### 3.2 Class L \u2014 the outbox\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE outbox (\n  op_id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY,   -- UUIDv7: idempotency key AND total order, client-generated\n  entity     TEXT NOT NULL,      -- geofence | alert_dismissal\n  entity_id  TEXT NOT NULL,\n  op         TEXT NOT NULL,      -- upsert | delete\n  payload    JSON NOT NULL,\n  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,\n  attempts   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,\n  last_error TEXT,\n  synced_at  TIMESTAMP           -- NULL = pending\n);\n```\n\nThree rules make this work:\n\n1. **The entity row and its outbox row are written in one transaction.** This is the whole reason the outbox exists. \"Saved locally but never queued\" is not a state the database can be in.\n2. **`op_id` is the server's idempotency key.** A retry after an ambiguous timeout is free. UUIDv7 sorts by creation time, so per-entity replay order is the key order \u2014 no sequence table.\n3. **Coalesce pending ops per `entity_id`.** A week in a basement dismissing and un-dismissing the same alert must not queue a week of operations.\n\n**Conflict resolution is per table, not global.** A blanket last-writer-wins is a smell, and the two Class L tables want opposite rules:\n\n- **`geofence` \u2192 LWW on `updated_at`.** A fence has one current shape; the most recent edit is the intended one.\n- **`alert` dismissal \u2192 earliest wins.** A dismissal is a monotonic acknowledgement \u2014 \"someone was on this at T\". LWW would let a device that reconnects later overwrite the fact that a colleague had already picked it up, which is exactly the information the dismissal exists to carry.\n\n### 3.3 Class D \u2014 disposable on purpose\n\nDerived tables are never synced, never backed up, and **never migrated**: any schema change drops and rebuilds them from R + L. That removes them from the migration surface entirely, which is most of the schema. It is also what makes the \u00a70 replay property operationally useful rather than merely elegant \u2014 \"rebuild\" is a supported, exercised code path, not a theory.\n\n### 3.4 Transaction boundaries and crash recovery\n\nIngest is deliberately **two** transactions, not one:\n\n1. append Class R rows \u00b7 advance `vehicle_signal_latest` \u00b7 advance the pull cursor\n2. derive alerts / transitions / trips \u00b7 advance `ingest_watermark`\n\nSplitting them keeps a long recompute from holding a write lock across the whole batch, and it enforces the ordering that matters: **the watermark advances last, so derived state is always behind the log and never ahead of it.**\n\nThe payoff is that there is no recovery routine. A crash between the two transactions leaves log rows with no derivation \u2014 which is byte-identical to the state during normal operation, and is repaired by the same \"derive from watermark\" call that every batch makes. Crash recovery is indistinguishable from ordinary incremental work, so it is tested by every test rather than by a special one nobody runs.\n\n### 3.5 Migrations on a device you cannot reach\n\n`schema_version` table, forward-only, applied on open before any query. The class split does most of the work: **D** is dropped and rebuilt, **R** can be re-pulled from cursor zero if a migration would be gnarly, and **L** \u2014 the only data with no upstream copy \u2014 is small enough to migrate by hand and carefully.\n\n### 3.6 What can actually be lost\n\nOnly unsynced outbox rows, and only if the database file becomes unopenable. Everything in R is re-pullable and everything in D is re-derivable. The mitigation is draining the outbox eagerly whenever connectivity exists, not mirroring it into a second store \u2014 a second store is a second thing to corrupt.\n\n### 3.7 The seam in this build\n\nThere is no backend (\u00a711), so: the cursor mechanism is real, because the packet simulator is a replayable, positioned source and ingest advances a genuine cursor against it. The outbox is **designed, not built** \u2014 it is one table and one drain loop, and until a server exists it would be a queue with no consumer. Swapping the simulator for an HTTP or MQTT source is a constructor argument; adding the outbox is the second commit after that.\n\n---\n\n'''\np = pathlib.Path(\"ARCHITECTURE.md\"); s = p.read_text()\nassert \"## 4. ## 4. Ingest

One transaction per batch, in the writer isolate:

1. **Dedupe within the batch** — keep `max(event_ts)` per `(vehicle_id, signal)`.
2. **Append** — `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Idempotency is now a database constraint, not a code path.
3. **Advance latest** — the only tricky upsert. A late packet must never clobber a newer reading:

```sql
INSERT INTO vehicle_signal_latest AS l (vehicle_id, signal, event_ts, value)
SELECT vehicle_id, signal, event_ts, value FROM batch
ON CONFLICT (vehicle_id, signal) DO UPDATE
  SET value = excluded.value, event_ts = excluded.event_ts
  WHERE excluded.event_ts > l.event_ts;
```

4. **Detect regression** — if `min(event_ts)` in the batch for a vehicle is older than its `ingest_watermark`, that vehicle needs a replay from `min(event_ts) − lookback`. Otherwise, incremental derivation from the watermark forward.
5. **Derive** — alerts, transitions, trips (§6, §7).
6. **Advance watermark**, commit, ping the UI.

Derivation runs **in SQL**, not Dart. Pulling the log into Dart to fold over it is precisely the in-memory-shadow the brief rules out, and it makes recompute over a large window unaffordable. The rules (hysteresis, debounce, thresholds) live in config tables so tests can vary them without touching SQL.

### Claude — 2026-09-12T07:47:21.703Z
Added as **§3 in [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md)** (renumbered the rest; §4 ingest now matches).

The whole answer is one classification: **who owns the truth for each row.** That decides sync direction, conflict rule, transaction boundary, and whether the table is disposable.

| Class | Tables | Sync | Conflict | On loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **R** remote-authoritative, immutable | `vehicle`, `signal_reading`, `location_fix` | pull, cursored | impossible by construction | re-pullable |
| **L** device-authored intent | `geofence`, alert dismissal | push, via outbox | per-table rule | **the only losable data** |
| **D** derived | `vehicle_signal_latest`, transitions, trips | never | n/a | dropped and rebuilt |

Four things that fall out of it:

**Natural key + cursor-in-the-same-transaction means at-least-once delivery is enough.** No exactly-once protocol. Crash between fetch and commit → re-pull, the constraint absorbs it. Dedupe is the *side effect* of the natural key, not its purpose.

**Class R is never row-updated.** DuckDB is OLAP — a per-row `UPDATE` on a 2 M-row table is a rewrite. Confining all mutation to the few-thousand-row tables isn't tidiness, it's the reason the schema is shaped this way.

**Outbox: entity row and outbox row in one transaction.** "Saved locally but never queued" stops being a representable state. `op_id` = UUIDv7 = idempotency key *and* replay order. Pending ops coalesce per entity so a week in a basement doesn't queue a week of work. Conflict rules are per-table, deliberately: geofence is LWW on `updated_at`, but **alert dismissal is earliest-wins** — a dismissal is a monotonic acknowledgement, and LWW would let a late-reconnecting device overwrite the fact that a colleague was already on it. A blanket LWW policy is the smell.

**Two transactions per ingest batch, watermark last.** Derived state is always behind the log, never ahead — so there is no recovery routine. A crash mid-batch leaves a state identical to normal operation, repaired by the same "derive from watermark" call every batch makes. Crash recovery gets exercised by every test instead of by a special one nobody runs.

Class D also drops out of the migration surface entirely (drop + rebuild), leaving only the small Class L tables needing real migrations.

skipped: the outbox is designed, not built — no backend in this scope (§11), so it'd be a queue with no consumer. The cursor is real, because the simulator is a positioned replayable source. Add the outbox the commit after a server exists.

/// A Dart library for interfacing with the DuckDB database engine.
///
/// This library provides a high-level, idiomatic Dart interface for
/// interacting with DuckDB, an in-process SQL OLAP database management system.
/// It includes support for executing queries, fetching results, and managing
/// transactions.
///
/// To use this library in your code:
/// ```dart
/// import 'package:dart_duckdb/dart_duckdb.dart';
/// ```
library;

import 'dart:ffi';

import 'package:dart_duckdb/src/api/connection.dart';
import 'package:dart_duckdb/src/api/database.dart';
import 'package:dart_duckdb/src/api/duckdb.dart' as api;

import 'package:dart_duckdb/src/ffi/load_library.dart' as load;

class BindingsWithLibrary {
  final Bindings bindings;
  final DynamicLibrary library;

  BindingsWithLibrary(this.library) : bindings = Bindings(library);
}

class DuckDB extends api.DuckDB {
  static DuckDB? instance;

  final BindingsWithLibrary _library;
  @override
  Bindings get bindings => _library.bindings;

  DuckDB._internal()
      : _library = BindingsWithLibrary(
          (load.open as load.OpenDynamicLibrary).openDuckDB(),
        );

  // Registers this class as the default instance of [DuckDB]
  static void registerWith() {
    DuckDB.instance = duckdb as DuckDB?;
  }

  /// Open a database, if the database does not exist, it will be created.
  /// Use :memory: to create an in-memory database.
  @override
  Future<Database> open(
    String filename, {
    Map<String, String>? settings,
  }) async {
    return DatabaseImpl.open(_library, dbname: filename, settings: settings)
        as Database;
  }

  /// Create a connection to the database.
  @override
  Future<Connection> connect(Database database, {String? id}) async {
    return ConnectionImpl.connect(database, id: id);
  }

  /// Create a connection to the database with a [TransferableDatabase].
  @override
  Future<Connection> connectWithTransferred(
    TransferableDatabase transferableDatabase, {
    String? id,
  }) async {
    return ConnectionImpl.connectWithTransferred(
      transferableDatabase as TransferableDatabaseImpl,
      id: id,
    );
  }

  /// The version of the duckdb library in used.
  @override
  String get version {
    return bindings.duckdb_library_version().readString();
  }
}

DuckDB? _duckDB;

/// Provides access to `duckdb` functions, such as opening new databases.
api.DuckDB get duckdb {
  return _duckDB ??= DuckDB._internal();
}

///
/// The default behavior can be overridden for a specific OS by using
/// [overrideFor]. To override the behavior on all platforms, use
/// [overrideForAll].
class OpenDynamicLibrary extends OpenLibrary {
  final Map<OperatingSystem, OpenLibraryLoader> _overriddenPlatforms = {};

  OpenDynamicLibrary._();

  /// Returns the current [OperatingSystem] as read from the [Platform] getters.
  OperatingSystem? get os {
    if (Platform.isAndroid) return OperatingSystem.android;
    if (Platform.isIOS) return OperatingSystem.iOS;
    if (Platform.isLinux) return OperatingSystem.linux;
    if (Platform.isMacOS) return OperatingSystem.macOS;
    if (Platform.isWindows) return OperatingSystem.windows;
    return null;
  }

  /// Opens the [DynamicLibrary] from which `duckdb.dart` is going to
  /// [DynamicLibrary.lookup] duckdb's methods that will be used. This method is
  /// meant to be called by `duckdb.dart` only.
  DynamicLibrary openDuckDB() {
    /// If the process already provides has the symbol, we can use it directly.
    /// This is useful when we have loaded the library and are now on an isolate.
    final process = DynamicLibrary.process();
    if (process.providesSymbol('duckdb_open')) {
      return process;
    }

    /// If we are in a test environment, we will load the library from the package.
    if (_isTestEnvironment()) {
      final prefix = '${Directory.current.path}/../duckdb';

      if (_overriddenPlatforms[OperatingSystem.windows] == null) {
        _overriddenPlatforms[OperatingSystem.windows] =
            () => DynamicLibrary.open(
                  '$prefix/windows/Libraries/release/duckdb.dll',
                );
      }

      if (_overriddenPlatforms[OperatingSystem.macOS] == null) {
        _overriddenPlatforms[OperatingSystem.macOS] = () => DynamicLibrary.open(
              '$prefix/macos/Libraries/release/libduckdb.dylib',
            );
      }

      if (_overriddenPlatforms[OperatingSystem.linux] == null) {
        _overriddenPlatforms[OperatingSystem.linux] = () => DynamicLibrary.open(
              '$prefix/linux/Libraries/release/libduckdb.so',
            );
      }
    }

    try {
      final forPlatform = _overriddenPlatforms[os];
      if (forPlatform != null) {
        return forPlatform();
      }
    } catch (error) {
      // ignore
    }

    return _defaultOpen();
  }

  /// Makes `duckdb.dart` use the [open] function when running on the specified
  /// [os]. This can be used to override the loading behavior on some platforms.
  /// To override that behavior on all platforms, consider using
  /// [overrideForAll].
  /// This method must be called before opening any database.
  ///
  /// When using the asynchronous API over isolates, [open] __must be__ a top-
  /// level function or a static method.
  @override
  void overrideFor(OperatingSystem os, String path) {
    _overriddenPlatforms[os] = () => DynamicLibrary.open(path);
  }

  /// Clears all associated open helpers for all platforms.
  @visibleForTesting
  @override
  void reset() {
    _overriddenPlatforms.clear();
  }
}

/// The instance managing different approaches to load the [DynamicLibrary] for
/// duckdb when needed. See the documentation for [OpenDynamicLibrary] to learn
/// how the default opening behavior can be overridden.
final OpenLibrary open = OpenDynamicLibrary._();
