{
  "command": "set -e\ncat > docs/05-geofences.md <<'MD'\n# 05 \u2014 Geofences\n\nCircular fences that are created, edited and deactivated in the app, and\nentry/exit detection folded out of the position log on every ingest batch.\n\nCovers the brief's \u00a73 D.\n\n## Files\n\n```\nlib/db/geofence_sql.dart      the detector, the fence upsert, the read queries\nlib/db/schema.dart            migration v2: containment table + four seed fences\nlib/features/geofence/\n  domain/entities/            geofence (+ geofence_occupancy \u00b7 geofence_visit)\n  domain/repositories/        geofence_repository\n  domain/usecases/            get_geofences \u00b7 save_geofence \u00b7 set_geofence_active\n  data/models/                geofence_model\n  data/datasources/           geofence_local_data_source (interface + DuckDB impl)\n  data/repositories/          geofence_repository_impl\n  presentation/               geofence_controller \u00b7 geofence_binding\n                              geofences_page \u00b7 geofence_editor_page\n  presentation/widgets/       geofence_tile \u00b7 zone_panel\n```\n\n## The detector\n\nOne query, eight stages, no row-at-a-time fold in Dart. That is not a\nperformance flourish \u2014 a Dart fold would have to re-read a vehicle's history\nto resume, and the resume is the hard part of this feature.\n\n| Stage | What it does | Brief's hard case |\n|---|---|---|\n| `probe` | fixes \u00d7 fences, gated on accuracy and on the fence being active **at the fix's event time** | inaccurate readings, geofence edits |\n| `opinion` | `IN` if `d \u2264 r \u2212 h`, `OUT` if `d \u2265 r + h`, `h = max(25 m, accuracy)`. In between: **no opinion at all** | GPS jitter |\n| `seeded` | the previous pass's state, injected as if it were the last opinionated fix before the window | incremental derivation |\n| `seq` | `lag` over the opinionated sequence only | |\n| `decided` | confirmed by **two consecutive opinionated fixes agreeing**, or one fix more than `2h` clear of the boundary | jitter vs. a genuine fast crossing |\n| `settled` | `last_value(\u2026 IGNORE NULLS)` carries the established zone forward | |\n| emit | a confirmation that disagrees with the established zone, stamped with the **first** fix of the pair | when did it actually cross |\n| confidence | `low` when the confirming pair straddles a gap > 30 min | missing intervals |\n\nThree of those are worth spelling out.\n\n**A fix in the band has no opinion, rather than a weak one.** That is what\nmakes the band genuinely inert. A truck parked on a boundary produces a run of\nfixes that say nothing at all, so there is nothing to flap between \u2014 the\nestablished zone simply persists. Carrying band fixes as votes would only move\nthe flapping somewhere subtler.\n\n**The transition is stamped with the first fix of the confirming pair**, not\nthe second. The vehicle crossed when it was first seen on the other side; the\nsecond fix is when *we* became sure. Stamping the second would push every\ncrossing late by one reporting interval, and every trip duration with it.\n\n**The escape hatch is scaled by the fix, not by the fence.** One fix more than\n`2h` past the boundary confirms alone, and because `h = max(25 m, accuracy)`, a\n5 m fix needs 50 m of clearance while a 100 m fix needs 200 m. A truck doing 60\nthrough the edge of a bay should not need a second fix to prove it left; a\ntruck reported vaguely should.\n\n**A cold start emits nothing.** The first confirmation *establishes* a zone.\nWe have learned where the truck is, not watched it go there, and inventing an\nENTRY would put a crossing in the record that never happened.\n\n## Resuming without re-reading the log\n\n`geofence_containment` holds, per (vehicle, fence), the confirmed zone and the\nlast fix that had an opinion at all. The detector injects that as a synthetic\nfirst row, so an ingest batch costs **two fixes of work instead of a vehicle's\nwhole history**. At 500 vehicles and a few thousand fixes each, the difference\nbetween those is the difference between the feature existing and not.\n\nThe table earns its place three times: it seeds the detector, it answers\n\"which fence is this truck in\" without touching the log, and it is what the\nlive per-fence counts are counted from.\n\n```\nscope \u2192 delete the range being rewritten \u2192 detect \u2192 upsert containment\n```\n\n**Late packets.** The scope query compares the batch's oldest fix against the\nvehicle's `ingest_watermark`. A batch that reaches back behind it invalidates\nthe seed \u2014 containment is the state *at* the watermark \u2014 so that vehicle is\nscoped to `-infinity` and replayed from the beginning of its log instead.\nThat is ARCHITECTURE.md \u00a74 step 4 with `t0` collapsed to the whole vehicle,\nbecause a per-fix `t0` would need a containment history we deliberately do not\nkeep. A full replay of one vehicle is a few thousand fixes; late packets are\nrare and already counted.\n\nThis runs **before** the watermark advances, because once it has moved the\ncomparison that detects a late batch is always false.\n\nThe property that makes all of this trustworthy is tested directly: feeding a\nroute one fix at a time, deriving after each, lands on byte-identical\ntransitions and containment to one pass over the finished log.\n\n## Overlapping fences\n\nDepot Bay 3 is seeded inside Whitefield Depot on purpose. Containment is\ntracked **per fence** \u2014 a truck in the bay is genuinely inside two \u2014 and there\nis no \"current geofence\" column anywhere, because under nesting there is no\nsuch thing.\n\nThe single value the UI wants is the **smallest radius containing the\nvehicle**, tie-broken by id: the most specific true answer (\u00a710, ambiguity 10).\nIt is a query, not a stored field, so it cannot go stale against containment.\n\nThis is also what stops a nested fence manufacturing a trip later: leaving a\nbay while still inside the depot is not a departure, and trips will key off\ncontainment *count* rather than individual fences (\u00a710, ambiguity 11).\n\n## Editing a fence\n\nActivation is time-versioned; geometry is not.\n\n* **Deactivating** sets `active_to`. Nothing is recomputed, because the fence\n  genuinely was live before that moment. The fence is kept, not deleted \u2014 a\n  trip that ended at a depot has to be able to name it a year later \u2014 and it\n  stays visible on the list, marked off, because a fence you cannot see is a\n  fence you cannot turn back on.\n* **Reactivating** starts a *new* active window rather than resuming the old\n  one, so the period it was off stays off in any recompute.\n* **Moving or resizing** re-derives that fence's whole history. Two answers on\n  record about whether a truck was inside would be worse than a slow save.\n\nSaving recomputes **every** fence, not just the one that changed. That is\ndeliberate: derived state is dropped and rebuilt (\u00a73.5), and one path that is\nalways right beats two that are usually right. A fence edit is rare and\nuser-initiated and can afford to be slow; a subtly wrong incremental path\ncannot. The editor says so before the button is pressed, and the screen shows\na progress bar while it runs.\n\n## The screens\n\n| Surface | What it shows |\n|---|---|\n| Geofences | Every fence: name, radius, centre, and how many vehicles are inside right now. Deactivated ones sorted last and marked off. New/edit/deactivate |\n| Geofence editor | Name, latitude, longitude, radius, validated rather than clamped |\n| Vehicle detail | The truck's current fence, and its last eight crossings with ages and a flag on the uncertain ones |\n| Fleet app bar | The way in |\n\nAn empty fence reads \"empty\" rather than `0`, and a truck in no fence reads\n\"On the road\" rather than an em dash \u2014 not being in a fence is a normal place\nfor a truck to be, not missing data.\n\nDeactivating asks for confirmation; reactivating does not. One stops the fence\njudging fixes from that moment on and leaves a gap in the history afterwards;\nthe other only undoes that.\n\n## Why no map\n\nTyped coordinates. Picking a point on a tile layer is the better interface and\nit is a cut, not an oversight (ARCHITECTURE.md \u00a711): every geofence rule in\nthis app is decided without one, and a tile layer would be the largest\ndependency in the project. The editor shows six decimal places so a centre can\nbe retyped exactly, which is the only reason the numbers are on screen.\n\nHaversine rather than DuckDB's spatial extension, for the same shape of\nreason: one expression against a loadable extension, a native dependency and a\n`GEOMETRY` column, for circles. If fences ever become polygons that trade\nflips.\n\n## Decisions\n\n| Decision | Why | Rejected |\n|---|---|---|\n| Band fixes have *no* opinion | Makes the band inert instead of moving the flapping | Carrying band fixes as weak votes |\n| Two-fix confirmation | One fix is jitter; two agreeing is a crossing | Bare `d < r` \u2014 a parked truck becomes dozens of trips |\n| Escape hatch scaled by accuracy | A fast crossing is real; a vague fix is not | A fixed metre threshold that is wrong for good and bad fixes alike |\n| Stamped with the first fix of the pair | That is when it crossed, not when we knew | The confirming fix \u2014 every crossing late by one interval |\n| Cold start establishes, does not emit | We learned where it is; we did not watch it arrive | An ENTRY on first sight, inventing a crossing |\n| Containment table | Two fixes of work per batch instead of a history; also answers the UI's two questions | Re-deriving from the log every batch |\n| Late batch replays the whole vehicle | The seed is only valid ahead of the watermark | A fixed lookback window, wrong at the edges |\n| Containment per fence, current fence as a query | Under nesting there is no single current fence | A `current_geofence_id` column |\n| Activation versioned, geometry not | Deactivating is free; moving is rare | Full geometry versioning \u2014 more table than this earns |\n| A fence edit recomputes everything | One path that is always right | An incremental path for the changed fence only |\n| Deactivated fences kept and listed | Trip history has to name them; hidden fences cannot be restored | Deleting, or hiding behind a filter |\n| Coordinates validated, not clamped | A mistyped longitude silently becoming 180 puts a depot in the Pacific | `clamp()` |\n\n## Tests\n\n| Claim | Test |\n|---|---|\n| A cold start establishes a zone and emits nothing; one ambiguous fix establishes nothing, one unambiguous fix establishes alone | `geofence_detector_test.dart` |\n| Two agreeing fixes confirm an entry, stamped with the first of the pair | same |\n| A round trip gives an entry and an exit | same |\n| One fix far past the boundary confirms alone; one just past the line does not | same |\n| A vehicle parked in the band never crosses | same |\n| An inaccurate fix is not evidence, and a mediocre fix widens the band it must clear | same |\n| A pair straddling a long gap is `low` confidence; an ordinary pair is `high` | same |\n| Fixes before a fence existed, or after it was deactivated, are not its business | same |\n| **Fix-by-fix derivation matches a single full replay** | same |\n| A late fix replayed from the beginning reveals the missed excursion and matches an in-order log exactly | same |\n| Re-deriving the same log is idempotent; a nested fence is tracked independently | same |\n| Migration v2 installs four fences, nested pair included | `geofence_store_test.dart` |\n| The detector runs inside ingest, through the real writer isolate, and moves the live count | same |\n| A nested fence counts the same vehicle twice over | same |\n| Renaming keeps the fence and its history; shrinking re-derives the vehicle out of it | same |\n| A new fence inherits no history; deactivation is kept, stops judging, and sorts last; reactivating starts a fresh window | same |\n| Migrations apply once and do not duplicate seed rows | `fleet_db_test.dart` |\n| The active count ignores deactivated fences; a blank fence is active from the injected clock | `geofence_controller_test.dart` |\n| A save pulses the database so the vehicle screens follow; a failure surfaces and clears the progress flag | same |\n| Size, centre and live count render; empty says \"empty\"; deactivated is listed and marked off | `geofence_page_test.dart` |\n| Deactivating asks first and can be cancelled; reactivating does not ask | same |\n| The editor refuses a blank name and an out-of-range coordinate; a valid fence is saved with its id kept | same |\n| The zone panel names the current fence and recent crossings; no fence reads \"On the road\"; a gap-confirmed crossing is flagged | `vehicle_detail_page_test.dart` |\n\n## Known limits\n\n* **No map.** See above. The editor is four fields.\n* **Circles only.** A polygon fence changes `probe` and nothing else in the\n  pipeline, but it changes the schema and the editor.\n* **A fence edit recomputes every fence.** Correct, and slow in proportion to\n  the whole log rather than to what changed.\n* **Containment has no history.** It holds the current state, which is why a\n  late packet replays the vehicle rather than the affected suffix. A\n  containment-at-time table would make that surgical and is the upgrade if\n  replays ever become common.\n* **The vehicle screen shows eight crossings.** The full history is in\n  `geofence_transition`; nothing renders it.\n* **`low` confidence is recorded and shown but drives nothing.** Trips will\n  inherit it; no rule currently treats an uncertain crossing differently.\nMD\nsed -i '' 's#| \u2014 | Geofences | \u00a73 D | Not built |#| 05 | [Geofences](05-geofences.md) | \u00a73 D | Built |#' docs/README.md\ngrep -n \"05\\|Geofences\\|Trips\" docs/README.md",

### User — 2026-09-13T18:06:40.284Z
Base directory for this skill: /Users/durgeshparekh/.claude/plugins/cache/ponytail/ponytail/4.8.4/skills/ponytail-review

Review diffs for unnecessary complexity. One line per finding: location, what
to cut, what replaces it. The diff's best outcome is getting shorter.

## Format

`L<line>: <tag> <what>. <replacement>.`, or `<file>:L<line>: ...` for
multi-file diffs.

Tags:

- `delete:` dead code, unused flexibility, speculative feature. Replacement: nothing.
- `stdlib:` hand-rolled thing the standard library ships. Name the function.
- `native:` dependency or code doing what the platform already does. Name the feature.
- `yagni:` abstraction with one implementation, config nobody sets, layer with one caller.
- `shrink:` same logic, fewer lines. Show the shorter form.

## Examples

❌ "This EmailValidator class might be more complex than necessary, have you
considered whether all these validation rules are needed at this stage?"

✅ `L12-38: stdlib: 27-line validator class. "@" in email, 1 line, real validation is the confirmation mail.`

✅ `L4: native: moment.js imported for one format call. Intl.DateTimeFormat, 0 deps.`

✅ `repo.py:L88: yagni: AbstractRepository with one implementation. Inline it until a second one exists.`

✅ `L52-71: delete: retry wrapper around an idempotent local call. Nothing replaces it.`

✅ `L30-44: shrink: manual loop builds dict. dict(zip(keys, values)), 1 line.`

## Scoring

End with the only metric that matters: `net: -<N> lines possible.`

If there is nothing to cut, say `Lean already. Ship.` and stop.

## Boundaries

Scope: over-engineering and complexity only. Correctness bugs, security holes,
and performance are explicitly out of scope. Route them to a normal review
pass, not this one. A single smoke test or `assert`-based
self-check is the ponytail minimum, not bloat, never flag it for deletion.
Does not apply the fixes, only lists them.
"stop ponytail-review" or "normal mode": revert to verbose review style.


ARGUMENTS: Do the code review, find all the critical issues and fix them all. Explain the issues and how did you fix this.

/// Isolate entry point. Top-level because `Isolate.spawn` cannot take a
/// closure that captures anything unsendable.
Future<void> _writerMain(_WriterBoot boot) async {
  final Connection conn;
  try {
    conn = await duckdb.connectWithTransferred(boot.transferable);
    await _createStagingTables(conn);
  } catch (error) {
    boot.reply.send(_WriterFailed(error.toString()));
    return;
  }

  final commands = ReceivePort();
  boot.reply.send(commands.sendPort);

  await for (final message in commands) {
    if (message is _Shutdown) {
      await conn.dispose();
      commands.close();
      message.reply.send(null);
      return;
    }
    if (message is _ToolRequest) {
      try {
        message.reply.send(
          _WriteResponse(payload: await _runTool(conn, message)),
        );
      } catch (error) {
        message.reply.send(_WriteResponse(error: error.toString()));
      }
      continue;
    }
    if (message is _GeofenceRequest) {
      try {
        await _saveGeofence(conn, message.row);
        message.reply.send(const _WriteResponse());
      } catch (error) {
        message.reply.send(_WriteResponse(error: error.toString()));
      }
      continue;
    }
    if (message is _AlertRequest) {
      try {
        await _applyAlertCommand(conn, message);
        message.reply!.send(const _WriteResponse());
      } catch (error) {
        message.reply!.send(_WriteResponse(error: error.toString()));
      }
      continue;
    }
    if (message is _SeedRequest) {
      try {
        message.reply.send(
          _WriteResponse(inserted: await _seedFleet(conn, message.vehicles)),
        );
      } catch (error) {
        message.reply.send(_WriteResponse(error: error.toString()));
      }
      continue;
    }
    final request = message as _WriteRequest;
    try {
      request.reply.send(
        _WriteResponse(

/// One leg between fences: left somewhere, arrived somewhere, or still going.
///
/// A trip is derived, never reported. Nothing in the packet stream says
/// "departed" — the vehicle only ever says where it is, and this is what falls
/// out of watching that against the fences (ARCHITECTURE.md §7.2).
class Trip {
  const Trip({
    required this.tripId,
    required this.vehicleId,
    required this.regNo,
    required this.startedAt,
    required this.isConfident,
    this.origin,
    this.destination,
    this.endedAt,
    this.distanceKm,
  });

  final String tripId;
  final String vehicleId;
  final String regNo;

  /// The fence the vehicle was last inside, or null when it was outside every
  /// fence we knew about at the time — a departure from nowhere in particular.
  final String? origin;

  /// Event time of the exit that emptied the vehicle's containment, which is
  /// when it actually left rather than when we became sure.
  final DateTime startedAt;

  /// Where it arrived, or null while it is still out there.
  final String? destination;

  /// When it arrived, or null. There is deliberately no timeout: a truck that
  /// never reports again keeps an open trip, because inventing an ending is
  /// worse than admitting we do not have one (§10, ambiguity 12).
  final DateTime? endedAt;

  /// Odometer delta across the leg, or null when the odometer did not report
  /// at one of the ends. For a running trip this is the distance **so far**.
  final double? distanceKm;

  /// False when either end was confirmed across a reporting gap longer than
  /// half an hour. The leg happened; its timing is approximate.
  final bool isConfident;

  bool get isRunning => endedAt == null;

  /// How long the leg took, or has taken so far.
  Duration elapsedAt(DateTime now) => (endedAt ?? now).difference(startedAt);
}

/// Cold-start measurement for the scale exercise (§8).
///
/// Deliberately global mutable state, and the only such state in the app.
/// Cold start is a property of the process, not of any object in it: the
/// stopwatch has to start before the object graph exists and stop inside a
/// widget that knows nothing about `main()`. Threading a holder between those
/// two points would be more machinery than the measurement.
///
/// A [Stopwatch] rather than two `DateTime.now()` readings, so this does not
/// become the one place that reaches for the wall clock the rest of the
/// codebase injects — and so a clock adjustment mid-launch cannot produce a
/// negative cold start.
library;

import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';

/// Started as the first statement of `main()`.
final coldStart = Stopwatch();

/// How long from `main()` to the first fleet list painted **with data**, or
/// null until that frame has been rasterised.
///
/// "With data" matters: stopping on the first frame would measure the
/// spinner, which is a number the app can always make small and which tells
/// nobody anything.
Duration? coldStartElapsed;

/// Stops the clock. Ignored after the first call — a later rebuild of the
/// fleet list is not a cold start.
void markFleetPainted() {
  if (coldStartElapsed != null || !coldStart.isRunning) return;
  coldStart.stop();
  coldStartElapsed = coldStart.elapsed;
  // Printed as well as shown on the scale screen: the number is wanted from a
  // terminal during a measurement run, and reading it off a screenshot of the
  // app that is being measured is how a measurement gets transcribed wrong.
  debugPrint('[scale] cold start ${coldStartElapsed!.inMilliseconds} ms');
}

/// Every leg the fleet has driven, running ones first.
class TripsPage extends GetView<TripsController> {
  const TripsPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: const Text('Trips'),
        actions: [
          Obx(
            () => Padding(
              padding: const EdgeInsets.only(right: 16),
              child: Center(child: Text('${controller.runningCount} running')),
            ),
          ),
        ],
      ),
      body: Obx(() {
        if (controller.error.isNotEmpty) {
          return Center(child: Text(controller.error.value));
        }
        if (controller.isLoading.value) {
          return const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());
        }
        if (controller.trips.isEmpty) {
          // Says what has to happen rather than just that nothing has. A trip
          // needs a vehicle to leave every fence it was in, which on a fresh
          // database has genuinely not happened yet.
          return const Center(
            child: Padding(
              padding: EdgeInsets.all(32),
              child: Text(
                'No trips yet. One starts when a vehicle leaves the last '
                'geofence it was inside.',
                textAlign: TextAlign.center,
              ),
            ),
          );
        }

        final now = controller.evaluatedAt.value ?? DateTime.now().toUtc();
        return ListView.separated(
          itemCount: controller.trips.length,
          separatorBuilder: (_, __) => const Divider(height: 1),
          itemBuilder: (_, index) =>
              TripTile(trip: controller.trips[index], now: now),
        );
      }),
    );
  }
}

/// Reads the fleet list out of DuckDB.
///
/// The whole read path is `vehicle` (500 rows) joined to
/// `vehicle_signal_latest` (500 x 6) and `signal_spec` (6). No scan of the
/// multi-million-row log happens here, which is the entire reason
/// `vehicle_signal_latest` is maintained on ingest.
abstract class FleetLocalDataSource {
  /// Rows for [filter] plus the count for every chip, read at instant [now].
  Future<FleetOverview> overview(FleetFilter filter, DateTime now);
}

/// DuckDB implementation.
class DuckDbFleetLocalDataSource implements FleetLocalDataSource {
  const DuckDbFleetLocalDataSource(this._read);

  /// The UI isolate's read connection. Sees an MVCC snapshot, so a commit in
  /// the writer never blocks the list.
  final Connection _read;

  @override
  Future<FleetOverview> overview(FleetFilter filter, DateTime now) async {
    try {
      // Two queries, both over the same CTE: the counts must span the whole
      // fleet while the rows are narrowed to one chip. Counting the returned
      // rows instead would make every chip read "the number you can see".
      final counts = await _counts(now);
      final vehicles = await _vehicles(filter, now);
      return FleetOverview(filter: filter, vehicles: vehicles, counts: counts);
    } catch (error) {
      throw LocalDatabaseException('fleet overview query failed', error);
    }
  }

  /// Count per status, plus the total for the "All" chip.
  Future<Map<FleetFilter, int>> _counts(DateTime now) async {
    final result = await _query(fleetCountsQuery, now);

    final counts = {for (final filter in FleetFilter.values) filter: 0};
    var total = 0;
    for (final row in result.fetchAll()) {
      final status = VehicleStatus.fromSql(row[0]! as String);
      final count = (row[1]! as num).toInt();
      total += count;
      counts[_filterFor(status)] = count;
    }
    counts[FleetFilter.all] = total;
    return counts;
  }

final fakeNow = DateTime.utc(2026, 1, 1, 12);

/// Serves a canned trip list.
class StubTripRepository implements TripRepository {
  StubTripRepository([this.trips = const []]);

  List<Trip> trips;

  /// How many times the controller has re-read the list.
  var loads = 0;

  /// When set, reads fail with this message.
  String? failWith;

  @override
  Future<Result<List<Trip>>> recent({int limit = 100}) async {
    loads++;
    if (failWith case final message?) return Err(DatabaseFailure(message));
    return Ok(trips);
  }

  @override
  Future<Result<List<Trip>>> forVehicle(
    String vehicleId, {
    int limit = 100,
  }) async {
    if (failWith case final message?) return Err(DatabaseFailure(message));
    return Ok(trips.where((trip) => trip.vehicleId == vehicleId).toList());
  }
}

/// Registers a real controller over [repository].
TripsController putStubTrips(StubTripRepository repository) {
  final pulse = Get.isRegistered<DatabasePulse>()
      ? Get.find<DatabasePulse>()
      : Get.put(DatabasePulse());
  return Get.put(
    TripsController(
      getRecentTrips: GetRecentTrips(repository),
      pulse: pulse,
      clock: FakeClock(fakeNow),
      refreshDebounce: Duration.zero,
    ),
  );
}

/// A completed trip, unless [endedAt] is cleared.
Trip testTrip({
  String tripId = 'v1|1',
  String vehicleId = 'v1',
  String regNo = 'KA01AA0001',
  String? origin = 'Whitefield Depot',
  String? destination = 'Electronic City Hub',
  DateTime? startedAt,
  DateTime? endedAt,
  double? distanceKm = 42.5,
  bool isConfident = true,
  bool running = false,
}) {
  final start = startedAt ?? fakeNow.subtract(const Duration(hours: 2));
  return Trip(
    tripId: tripId,
    vehicleId: vehicleId,
    regNo: regNo,
    origin: origin,
    destination: running ? null : destination,
    startedAt: start,
    endedAt: running ? null : (endedAt ?? start.add(const Duration(hours: 1))),
    distanceKm: distanceKm,
    isConfident: isConfident,
  );
}

  return (_bytesOf(row[0]), _bytesOf(row[1]));
}

/// Turns DuckDB's human-readable size into bytes.
///
/// The pragma returns text — "0 bytes", "12.3 MiB" — so this reads the number
/// and the one letter that scales it. Every unit the pattern matches is in
/// [_scale], and anything it does not match reports 0 rather than a wrong
/// number: a size silently off by 1024 is worse than one obviously missing.
int _bytesOf(Object? value) {
  if (value is num) return value.toInt();
  final match = _size.firstMatch(value.toString().trim());
  if (match == null) return 0;
  return (double.parse(match.group(1)!) * _scale[match.group(2)]!).round();
}

/// The multiplier for each unit letter [_bytesOf] understands.
const _scale = <String, int>{
  '': 1,
  'K': 1024,
  'M': 1048576,
  'G': 1073511627776 ~/ 1024 * 1024,
  'T': 1099511627776,
};

/// Built **from** [_scale], so the letters the pattern accepts and the letters
/// that have a multiplier cannot drift apart. Spelling the class out by hand
/// is how a `T` the pattern matched met a map that stopped at `G`, and turned
/// a large database into a null-check crash instead of a number.
final _size = RegExp(r'^([\d.]+)\s*([' + _scale.keys.join() + r']?)');

**1. `_bytesOf` crashed on a large database** — `lib/db/retention_sql.dart`

The regex accepted `[KMGT]?`, the multiplier map went `'' K M G`. A `pragma_database_size()` returning `"1.2 TiB"` matched `T`, looked it up, got null, and `scale[...]!` threw — inside the retention action's own result reporting, so the compaction would have succeeded and the screen would have shown an exception. The doc comment directly above claimed unrecognised units report 0, which was never true for the one unit that could hit it.

Fixed the bug class rather than the instance: `_scale` now carries `T`, and the pattern is built *from* `_scale.keys`, so the accepted alphabet and the keys with multipliers cannot drift apart again. The `!` is now unreachable by construction, which is why I left a test out — there's nothing left to disagree. Checked the parser standalone against `0 bytes` / `12.0 MiB` / `2.5 GiB` / `1.0 TiB` / garbage before wiring it back in.

**2. A three-layer read path with no caller** — `trip_repository.dart`, `trip_repository_impl.dart`, `trip_local_data_source.dart`, `trip_doubles.dart`

`forVehicle` existed as an interface method, an implementation, a data-source method, a DuckDB implementation and a stub override. Nothing in `lib/` called any of it: vehicle detail runs `vehicleTripsQuery` on its own connection on purpose, documented at `vehicle_detail_local_data_source.dart:214` — one screen, one snapshot, one round trip. So the repository path was built for a caller that was deliberately never going to exist.

Deleted all five. The one test covering it (`trip_store_test.dart`, "one vehicle reads the same trips as the fleet list") was asserting through the dead path, so it proved nothing about the app; repointed it at `DuckDbVehicleDetailLocalDataSource.detail()`, which is what actually runs in production. The test now pins something real — that the two screens agree — instead of pinning the stub.

**3. Orphaned doc comment** — `scale_controller.dart`

"Stops the simulator feed…" sat above a blank line, above `static const vehicles`. Dart attaches the *last* doc comment, so it documented nothing and `vehicles` read as if it were about pausing the feed. Moved it onto `_pauseFeed`, 45 lines down, which had none.

**4. The UI stated numbers the code doesn't produce** — `scale_controller.dart`, `scale_page.dart`

Two stale claims left over from when the backfill spread 700 ticks across two weeks:

- "Spread across seven days" / "spread over seven days" — the cadence is 10 s, so it's ~2 h of dense history. `backfill_sql.dart` and `docs/07-scale.md` already said two hours; the screen contradicted both.
- The retention card said "Readings older than seven days" while the result row under it printed `Kept at full resolution: 60 min` whenever `SCALE_KEEP_MINUTES` was set — the card and its own output disagreeing on screen.

Now the backfill card says "at a ten-second cadence" and the retention card says "past the window below", deferring to the row that reports the window the run actually used.

**5. Running trips printed their duration twice** — `trip_tile.dart`

`elapsedAt(now)` is `(endedAt ?? now) - startedAt`, and the row also appended `now.difference(startedAt)` as "… ago". For an open trip those are the same subtraction, so a row read `running 2h · 12.0 km · 2h ago` — two identical numbers side by side invite the reader to assume one of them means something else. The "ago" clause now only renders on completed trips, where "took 1h · 3h ago" says two different things.

### Claude — 2026-09-14T02:34:53.677Z

### Claude — 2026-09-14T02:35:10.294Z
An alert is an **episode** stored as one row in `alert`, not a flag on the vehicle. It has a start (`raised_at`), can escalate while it's open (`escalated_at`), and ends only when recovery is actually observed (`resolved_at`). Dismissal is a separate pair of columns (`dismissed_at`, `dismiss_reason`) that records a person's decision. It hides the row but doesn't end the episode.

An alert shows on screen when both `resolved_at IS NULL` and `dismissed_at IS NULL` ([alert_sql.dart:24](lib/db/alert_sql.dart:24)). The fleet badge, the alerts list and vehicle detail all use that same check.

## 1. Raising, escalating and resolving: the evaluator

`evaluateAlerts(conn, now)` ([alert_sql.dart:252](lib/db/alert_sql.dart:252)) runs on the writer isolate inside every ingest transaction, before the watermark moves. It runs four statements in a fixed order:

1. **Read what's visible.** It fills a temp table `staging_alert_condition` from `vehicle_signal_latest`, using **fresh** readings only (each signal's `max_age_sec` from `signal_spec`). Each row gets one of three outcomes:
   - `severity` is set: the reading breaches a threshold right now.
   - `cleared = true`: the reading is back inside the threshold by more than `alertClearBand` (2 units).
   - Neither: the reading is fresh but inside the hysteresis band, so nothing changes.

   A vehicle with no fresh reading gets **no row at all**.
2. **Resolve** open episodes whose row says `cleared`. It checks `EXISTS … AND c.cleared`, not `NOT EXISTS`. Missing data is not evidence of recovery: a truck that goes silent at 5 % SOC keeps its alert.
3. **Rescore** open episodes in place. SOC dropping from 18 % to 8 % is the *same* alert turning critical, not a second alert. `escalated_at` is stamped only on the way up.
4. **Raise** a new episode for any breach that has no open episode. The `NOT EXISTS` check makes this idempotent. The id `vehicle|type|epoch_ms(now)` is derived rather than random, so a replay produces the same row.

Resolve runs before raise, so a condition that clears and re-triggers within one batch closes the old episode instead of silently extending it. The whole pass is a pure function of `vehicle_signal_latest` and `now`: running it twice changes nothing the second time.

The hysteresis band exists because of a measurement: without it, a truck idling at 45.2 °C produced seven episodes in 114 seconds.

## 2. Dismissal

```
AlertCard → dismissWithReason()                 alerts_page.dart:57
  → showDismissReasonSheet()                    "I am on it" / "Wrong alert" / "Something else…"
  → AlertsController.dismiss()                  clock-injected `at`
  → DismissAlert use case → AlertRepositoryImpl reason.stored(note) → 'on_it' or 'other: <text>'
  → AlertLocalDataSource → TelemetryWriter.dismissAlert()
  → writer isolate: _applyAlertCommand()        BEGIN; UPDATE alert SET dismissed_at, dismiss_reason; COMMIT
```

- **The single writer does it.** DuckDB allows one writer, so the dismissal goes through the same isolate as ingest. It gets its own transaction, so a failing ingest batch can never roll back a user's action.
- **Cancelling the sheet cancels the dismissal.** If someone picks "Something else…" and then backs out of the text field, nothing is written. That isn't treated as "dismiss with no reason".
- **Free text shares the reason column** (`other: <note>`), so no migration was needed for it.
- **The screen refreshes right away:** `_settle()` reloads the list first and then pings `DatabasePulse`, so the fleet badge updates too.

## 3. Undo

After a successful write, the page shows a 5-second `SnackBar` with **UNDO** ([alerts_page.dart:74](lib/features/alerts/presentation/pages/alerts_page.dart:74)). Tapping it calls `controller.undo(alertId)`, which goes through the writer and runs `restoreAlert`: `SET dismissed_at = NULL, dismiss_reason = NULL`.

The main design decision: **the dismissal is on disk before the snackbar appears.** An alternative was to hide the row in memory for five seconds and only commit if the user doesn't undo. That was rejected. In a local-first app the database is the truth, and if the app is killed during the window, the user's explicit action should survive.

Undo is a separate SQL statement rather than `dismissAlert` with null parameters, because writing `= NULL` in the SQL text is safer than binding a typed NULL through the prepared-statement API.

## 4. How dismissal and the lifecycle interact

| Event after a dismissal | Result |
|---|---|
| Reading recovers past the band | Episode **resolves** anyway. Dismissal doesn't stop it ending. |
| Warning escalates to critical | **Dismissal is cleared** and the alert reappears. "I am on it" at 18 % isn't consent to ignore 8 %. |
| Critical walks back to warning | Severity drops in place; the dismissal (if any) stays. |
| Truck stops reporting | Nothing changes: no fresh row means no resolve and no rescore. |
| New breach after resolution | A **new** episode with a new id; the old dismissal doesn't carry over. |

So a dismissal survives recovery but not escalation. `test/features/alerts/alert_evaluator_test.dart` pins those rules, and the full reasoning is in [docs/04-alerts.md](docs/04-alerts.md).

## One behaviour to know before defending it

Undo is only limited by the UI. The snackbar disappears after 5 s, but the database doesn't check that the undo arrives within 5 s of the dismissal, and `restoreAlert` has no condition on the alert's state. In practice that's harmless:
- If the alert escalated in the meantime, its dismissal is already null.
- If it resolved, it stays hidden because `resolved_at` is set.

The DuckDB side will accept a late undo, though, so if it ever comes from anywhere other than that snackbar, it would need a `WHERE dismissed_at >= now - 5s` guard.

import 'dart:isolate';

import 'package:dart_duckdb/dart_duckdb.dart';

import 'schema.dart';

/// The embedded database. One instance per process — DuckDB takes a file lock,
/// so extra isolates attach through [transferable] rather than reopening.
///
/// This library is deliberately Flutter-free so the DB tests run on the plain
/// Dart VM. The app supplies the file path (see `lib/main.dart`).
class FleetDb {
  FleetDb._(this._db, this.read);

  final Database _db;

  /// Read-only-by-convention connection for the UI isolate. DuckDB is MVCC,
  /// so this sees a consistent snapshot while the writer commits.
  final Connection read;

  /// Pass to [inIsolate] to get a connection on another isolate.
  TransferableDatabase get transferable => _db.transferable;

  /// Opens [path] (`:memory:` for a throwaway db) and migrates it forward.
  static Future<FleetDb> open(String path) async {
    final db = await duckdb.open(path);
    final conn = await duckdb.connect(db);
    await _migrate(conn);
    return FleetDb._(db, conn);
  }

  /// Runs [job] on its own isolate with its own connection.
  ///
  /// [job] must be a top-level or static function: it is sent across an
  /// isolate boundary, so anything it closes over has to be sendable too.
  static Future<R> inIsolate<R>(
    TransferableDatabase transferable,
    Future<R> Function(Connection) job,
  ) {
    return Isolate.run(() async {
      final conn = await duckdb.connectWithTransferred(transferable);
      try {
        return await job(conn);
      } finally {
        await conn.dispose();
      }
    });
  }

  Future<void> close() async {
    await read.dispose();
    await _db.dispose();
  }
}

/// Forward-only migrations, applied in one transaction each so a crash
/// mid-upgrade leaves the previous version intact rather than a half-schema.
Future<void> _migrate(Connection conn) async {
  await conn.execute(
    'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_version (version INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)',
  );
  final result = await conn.query(
    'SELECT coalesce(max(version), 0) FROM schema_version',
  );
  final applied = (result.fetchOne()!.first as num).toInt();

  for (var version = applied + 1; version <= migrations.length; version++) {
    await conn.execute('BEGIN TRANSACTION');
    try {
      await conn.execute(migrations[version - 1]);
      await conn.execute('INSERT INTO schema_version VALUES ($version)');
      await conn.execute('COMMIT');
    } catch (_) {
      await conn.execute('ROLLBACK');
      rethrow;
    }
  }
}

/// Runs a parameterised statement and discards the result.
///
/// Here rather than beside any one feature's SQL because three of them need
/// it. Parameters rather than interpolation because most of these carry a
/// timestamp, and interpolating one into SQL text is how time zones get lost.
Future<void> execPrepared(
  Connection conn,
  String sql,
  List<Object?> params,
) async {
  final statement = await conn.prepare(sql);
  try {
    statement.bindParams(params);
    await statement.execute();
  } finally {
    await statement.dispose();
  }
}

## 0. The one idea

> **Derived state is a pure fold over an append-only event log. Late or duplicate data is handled by replaying the affected suffix, never by patching.**

Everything hard in this brief — duplicates, out-of-order packets, GPS jitter, backlog dumps, geofence edits, trip revision — collapses into that sentence. Alerts, geofence transitions and trips are *never* mutated in place by an incoming packet. They are recomputed from the log for the window the packet touches. Recompute is idempotent because the derivation is a pure function of `(event log ∩ [t0, ∞), config)`.

The corollary is the invariant worth testing above all others:

> Shuffle the packet stream arbitrarily, replay duplicates, and the final derived state must be byte-identical to the in-order replay.

---

### Isolates

DuckDB is a single-writer, MVCC embedded engine. One process, so multiple connections against one instance are fine — readers get a snapshot while the writer commits.

- **Writer isolate** (`TelemetryWriter`) — owns ingest, derivation, backfill. Everything that mutates runs here, serialised, in transactions. Spawned once at startup and kept: `Isolate.run` per batch would cost more than the write it performs. Requests carry their own reply port, so there is no request-id bookkeeping.
- **UI isolate** — read-only connection, queries on demand and after each batch. A 3-hour backlog dump must not repaint the fleet list 500 times, so once the fleet list exists this becomes a *debounced* change ping (250 ms) rather than a refresh per batch.

`dart_duckdb` exposes a transferable database handle for exactly this. Ingest batches are bounded (≤ 5k rows / 200 ms per transaction) so a backlog dump never holds a write lock long enough to stall reads.

---

## 2. Schema

Location is deliberately **not** a signal. Pairing `lat` and `lon` rows by timestamp is pointless work, and every geofence query wants them side by side.

  signal     TEXT NOT NULL,        -- soc | speed | battery_temp | odometer | range_km | ignition
  event_ts   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,   -- from the packet
  value      DOUBLE  NOT NULL,     -- booleans as 0/1
  ingest_ts  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,   -- audit only, never drives logic
  PRIMARY KEY (vehicle_id, signal, event_ts)

CREATE TABLE location_fix (

### Claude — 2026-09-14T04:31:59.621Z
The schema follows from one idea ([ARCHITECTURE.md §0](ARCHITECTURE.md)): **the database stores only what the trucks reported and what the operator decided. Everything else is calculated from those two and can be rebuilt at any time.**

## The tables, grouped by who owns the data

There are 12 tables in [lib/db/schema.dart](lib/db/schema.dart), plus `schema_version` for migrations. Each belongs to one of three groups, and the group decides how the table is written, synced and migrated.

### R: facts from the trucks (never edited)

| Table | Key | Why it looks like this |
|---|---|---|
| `vehicle` | `vehicle_id` | The roster: 500 small rows. |
| `signal_reading` | `(vehicle_id, signal, event_ts)` | **The event log, and the only large table** (2 M+ rows). One row per reading; a tall table rather than a column per signal, so adding a signal doesn't need a migration. |
| `location_fix` | `(vehicle_id, event_ts)` | GPS positions kept apart from the signals. Latitude and longitude always arrive together, and every geofence query wants them side by side; storing them as two signals would mean re-pairing them by timestamp in every query. |

Why these rules:
- **Natural keys plus `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.** The key is the thing that makes a reading unique. A duplicate packet hits the primary key and is silently skipped, so duplicate handling is a database constraint rather than Dart code, and receiving a packet twice is harmless.
- **Never updated or deleted during normal use.** DuckDB is a column store, so an `UPDATE` on a 2-million-row table rewrites a lot of data. All row-level changes are kept in tables of a few thousand rows.
- **Two timestamps.** `event_ts` is when the truck measured the value, and every rule uses it. `ingest_ts` is when the row arrived; it's kept for auditing and drives nothing, so a delayed packet can't make old data look fresh.

### L: decisions made on the device

| Table / columns | Why |
|---|---|
| `geofence` | Fences the operator creates. `active_from` / `active_to` means deactivating a fence closes its window instead of deleting the row, so an old trip can still name the depot it ended at. |
| `alert.dismissed_at`, `alert.dismiss_reason` | A person's decision about an alert. |

This is the only data with no copy anywhere else, which is why it's kept small. The design has an outbox table for syncing it to a server (§3.2), but it isn't built, because there is no server.

### Config

| Table | Why |
|---|---|
| `signal_spec` | Thresholds and freshness windows stored as rows, not Dart constants. The NORMAL / ALERT / STALE labels, the alert evaluator and the UI units all read the same row, so they can't disagree. |

### D: calculated from R + L, rebuildable

| Table | Size | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| `vehicle_signal_latest` | ~3 000 rows | **This is what makes the fleet list fast.** The list reads 500 × 6 rows instead of scanning the 2 M-row log. It's updated during ingest, and a late packet can't overwrite a newer reading (`WHERE excluded.event_ts > l.event_ts`). |
| `alert` | small | One row per episode. The id is built from vehicle, type and time rather than generated randomly, so a replay produces the same row. |
| `geofence_transition` | small | ENTRY / EXIT events calculated from `location_fix`. |
| `geofence_containment` | 500 × fences | Where each truck currently stands relative to each fence. The detector resumes from here instead of re-reading history, and live fence counts are counted from it. |
| `trip` | small | Calculated from the transitions. The id is `vehicle_id|start_ts`. |
| `ingest_watermark` | 500 rows | How far calculation has got for each vehicle. |
| `signal_rollup` | grows slowly | 5-minute summaries (count, min, max, avg, last) of readings older than the retention window. |

The main point: **these tables are never repaired by hand.** A late packet deletes the affected calculated rows and recalculates them; changing a geofence recalculates everything. Recalculating is always safe because it's a pure function of the log. The ingest test checks this directly: the same packets shuffled, re-batched and partly redelivered must produce byte-identical results.

The one exception is `signal_rollup`. Its source rows have been deleted, so it can't be rebuilt — which is why [docs/07-scale.md](docs/07-scale.md) spells out what retention loses.

## Temporary tables (on the writer's connection only)

`staging_signal`, `staging_location`, `staging_geo_scope`, `staging_alert_condition`. They're `TEMP`, so they never touch the file.

- An ingest batch is bulk-loaded into staging with DuckDB's appender, then moved into the real tables with a few set-based SQL statements. There's no statement per row and no escaping values into SQL text.
- Several statements share one working set (for example "which vehicles to recalculate"). A CTE only lasts for one statement; a table can be shared, so the definition is written once and can't drift between copies.

## How a batch moves through it

```
packets → staging_* (TEMP)
  tx 1: signal_reading, location_fix  (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING)
        vehicle_signal_latest         (newer readings only)
  tx 2: alert → geofence_transition / containment → trip
        ingest_watermark              (always last)
UI isolate reads its own snapshot → vehicle_signal_latest, alert, trip …
```

- **Two transactions.** A long recalculation doesn't hold the write lock while the batch's rows go in.
- **The watermark moves last**, so calculated state can lag behind the log but is never ahead of it. A crash between the two transactions leaves the same state as normal operation, and the next batch catches up with no special recovery code.
- **One writer, one reader.** DuckDB allows a single writer, so every write goes through one long-lived isolate in order. The UI has its own read connection, and MVCC gives it a consistent snapshot, so a commit never blocks the list.

## Why DuckDB for this workload

- The heavy queries are analytical: bucketing SOC history, the latest reading per signal, window functions over location fixes. That's exactly what a column store is built for, and DuckDB's SQL has what the calculations need: `ASOF JOIN` for the trip odometer, `time_bucket`, `arg_max`, `QUALIFY`.
- **All calculation happens in SQL, not Dart.** The brief rules out an in-memory copy, and pulling the log into Dart would recreate one. It would also make recalculating a large window too slow.
- The trade-off is that row updates are expensive, and the grouping above exists to work around that.

## Migrations

- The schema lives as Dart strings, not a `.sql` asset file, because migrations run on the writer isolate and isolates can't read the asset bundle.
- A `migrations` list plus a `schema_version` table. Changes are forward-only, and each migration runs in its own transaction, so a crash leaves the previous version intact.
- `_v2` and `_v3` were added as new migrations rather than edits to `_v1`, because `_v1` had already been applied to a real database file.

## Where the build differs from ARCHITECTURE.md

- **No outbox and no sync cursor table.** §3 describes them, but without a server they would have nothing to talk to (§3.7). The only position the code tracks is `ingest_watermark`.
- **Calculated tables aren't dropped and rebuilt on migration yet.** §3.3 designs that, but so far every migration has only added tables, so nothing has needed it.
- **Deactivating a fence while a truck is inside it** leaves that truck's containment count above zero forever, so it never gets a trip. This is ambiguity 16 in ARCHITECTURE.md and isn't fixed.

## How the tables relate

```
vehicle ─┬─< signal_reading >── signal_spec
         ├─< location_fix
         ├─< vehicle_signal_latest >── signal_spec
         ├─< alert
         ├─< trip >── geofence   (origin, dest)
         ├─< geofence_transition >── geofence
         ├─< geofence_containment >── geofence
         ├─< signal_rollup >── signal_spec
         └── ingest_watermark     (1 : 1)
```

## Why there are no foreign keys

Nothing in the code or docs explains this, so an interviewer will probably ask. Here is the defence I'd give, with the parts I haven't verified marked.

- **Cost on the busiest write.** A foreign key on `signal_reading.vehicle_id` means an extra lookup in `vehicle` for every row of every batch, and during backfill for all 2 M rows. The primary key already costs one index check per row for duplicate rejection.
- **DuckDB's foreign keys are restrictive.** They have no `ON DELETE CASCADE`, and a referenced parent row can't be deleted or have its key changed. For example, deactivating a fence is safe because the row stays, but if a fence were ever deleted or re-keyed, the delete-and-rebuild of transitions and trips would have to run in exactly the right order.
- **Integrity comes from how rows are written instead.** The calculated tables (`alert`, `trip`, `geofence_transition`, `geofence_containment`, `vehicle_signal_latest`) are only ever produced by SQL that joins to their parents, so they can't reference a vehicle or fence that doesn't exist. Geofences are deactivated rather than deleted, so trips never lose the fence they point to.
- **The real gap is the log tables.** `signal_reading` and `location_fix` would accept a packet for a `vehicle_id` that isn't in the roster. Before claiming that's harmless, I'd check what ingest does with an unknown vehicle — I haven't.

A one-line comment on the v1 schema recording this decision would stop it looking like an oversight.

Example — "Why React component re-render?"

- full: "Pool reuse open DB connections. No new connection per request. Skip handshake overhead."

/// Idempotent, so the app can call it unconditionally on every launch.
Future<int> _seedFleet(Connection conn, List<List<Object?>> vehicles) async {
  await conn.execute('''
    CREATE TEMP TABLE IF NOT EXISTS staging_vehicle (
      vehicle_id TEXT, reg_no TEXT, model TEXT
    );
    DELETE FROM staging_vehicle;
  ''');

  final appender = await conn.append('staging_vehicle', null);
  try {
    for (final row in vehicles) {
      for (final value in row) {
        appender.append(value);
      }
      appender.endRow();
    }
    appender.flush();
  } finally {
    appender.dispose();
  }

  return _countOf(conn, '''
    INSERT INTO vehicle
    SELECT * FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ON (vehicle_id) * FROM staging_vehicle)
    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
  ''');
}

/// Appends the batch to the event log.
///
/// `DISTINCT ON` collapses duplicates *within* the batch; `ON CONFLICT DO
/// NOTHING` against the natural primary key collapses duplicates against
/// everything already on disk. Re-delivering a packet is therefore a no-op
/// enforced by the database, not by application code.
Future<int> _appendSignalLog(Connection conn) async {
  return _countOf(conn, '''
    INSERT INTO signal_reading
    SELECT vehicle_id, signal, event_ts, value, CAST(now() AS TIMESTAMP)
    FROM (
      SELECT DISTINCT ON (vehicle_id, signal, event_ts) *
      FROM staging_signal
      ORDER BY vehicle_id, signal, event_ts
    )
    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
  ''');
}

/// Same contract as [_appendSignalLog], for position reports.
Future<int> _appendLocationLog(Connection conn) async {
  return _countOf(conn, '''
    INSERT INTO location_fix
    SELECT vehicle_id, event_ts, lat, lon, accuracy_m, CAST(now() AS TIMESTAMP)
    FROM (
      SELECT DISTINCT ON (vehicle_id, event_ts) *
      FROM staging_location
      ORDER BY vehicle_id, event_ts
    )
    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
  ''');
}

/// Moves the latest-value table forward.
///
/// The `WHERE excluded.event_ts > l.event_ts` guard is the entire late-packet
/// story for the read path: a packet that arrives late but measures an older
/// moment updates the log and leaves the current value alone.
Future<void> _advanceLatest(Connection conn) async {
  await conn.execute('''
    INSERT INTO vehicle_signal_latest AS l
    SELECT vehicle_id, signal, event_ts, value
    FROM (
      SELECT DISTINCT ON (vehicle_id, signal) *
      FROM staging_signal
      ORDER BY vehicle_id, signal, event_ts DESC

### Claude — 2026-09-14T04:53:42.216Z
Checked [schema.dart](lib/db/schema.dart) and the ingest SQL. I disagree with part of this, so I haven't changed any code.

## Correction first

- **The PK exists.** It's `PRIMARY KEY (vehicle_id, signal, event_ts)` at [schema.dart:26](lib/db/schema.dart:26). A composite PK is valid SQL: a primary key can be one column or several.
- **No FK is declared.** Grep finds no `REFERENCES` or `FOREIGN KEY` anywhere, so the earlier answer was right. The FK is only implied.
- **A column can be in the PK and be an FK at the same time.** In `signal_reading`, `vehicle_id` is part of the PK and also refers to `vehicle`. `signal` is part of the PK and also refers to `signal_spec`. These roles don't conflict.

## Why not `signal_reading_id` as PK

A reading is identified by "this truck, this signal, this moment". That is the natural key.

1. **Duplicates are the main risk.** Devices resend packets, and the same `(v1, soc, 10:00:00)` can arrive twice. With the natural PK, `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` ([telemetry_writer_isolate.dart:436](lib/features/telemetry_ingest/data/datasources/telemetry_writer_isolate.dart:436)) drops the copy. With a generated id, each copy gets a new id, both rows are stored, and trips, alerts and rollups count the reading twice.
2. **You would still need `UNIQUE(vehicle_id, signal, event_ts)`** to stop that. So a surrogate id adds a column and a second index, and blocks nothing extra.
3. **Nothing looks up one reading by id.** All reads are "vehicle X, signal Y, time range", which is a prefix of the composite PK.
4. **Sync.** A number generated on one device can clash with the same number on another device or the server. The natural key means the same thing everywhere.

Rule used: **natural key when the data has one, surrogate when it doesn't.**

## All tables, reviewed

| Table | PK | Logical FKs | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `schema_version` | `version` | none | ok |
| `vehicle` | `vehicle_id` | none | ok, parent |
| `signal_spec` | `signal` | none | ok, parent |
| `signal_reading` | `(vehicle_id, signal, event_ts)` | `vehicle_id`→vehicle, `signal`→signal_spec | keep, dedupe key |
| `location_fix` | `(vehicle_id, event_ts)` | `vehicle_id`→vehicle | keep, one position per truck per moment |
| `geofence` | `geofence_id` | none | surrogate is right: created on device, no natural key, name can change |
| `vehicle_signal_latest` | `(vehicle_id, signal)` | both | keep; the PK enforces one "latest" row per pair, which an id would not |
| `alert` | `alert_id` | `vehicle_id`→vehicle | keep; same truck and type can raise many times, so one row per episode |
| `geofence_transition` | `(vehicle_id, geofence_id, event_ts)` | `vehicle_id`→vehicle, `geofence_id`→geofence | keep, dedupe on replay |
| `trip` | `trip_id` | `vehicle_id`→vehicle, `origin_geofence_id` / `dest_geofence_id`→geofence (nullable) | keep |
| `ingest_watermark` | `vehicle_id` | `vehicle_id`→vehicle (1:1) | ok |
| `geofence_containment` | `(vehicle_id, geofence_id)` | both | keep, one state per pair |
| `signal_rollup` | `(vehicle_id, signal, bucket_ts)` | `vehicle_id`, `signal` | keep; retention re-runs upsert on it |

`trip_id` and `alert_id` are built from the data, not random:
- `trip_id` = `vehicle_id|epoch_ms(start)` ([trip_sql.dart:144](lib/db/trip_sql.dart:144))
- `alert_id` = `vehicle_id|type|epoch_ms` ([alert_sql.dart:194](lib/db/alert_sql.dart:194))

When trips are rebuilt, the same trip gets the same id, and nothing downstream sees a change.

**Verdict: no PK needs changing.**

## Why the FKs aren't declared (DuckDB-specific)

1. **One bad row would fail the whole batch.** Ingest is a single set-based `INSERT … SELECT`. If one packet has an unknown `vehicle_id`, the FK check fails the statement and transaction 1 rolls back. The valid readings from the other 499 trucks in that batch are lost too.
2. **Every child insert checks the parent's index.** That cost lands on the hot path (500×6 rows every tick) and on backfill (millions of rows).
3. **DuckDB has no `ON DELETE CASCADE`**, and it refuses to delete a parent row that still has children.
4. **FKs can't be added to existing tables.** DuckDB has no `ALTER TABLE ADD FOREIGN KEY`, so a migration would have to rebuild and copy the whole log.

## Real gap: orphans

Ingest doesn't filter today. A reading for a vehicle not in `vehicle`, or a signal not in `signal_spec`, gets stored silently. Fix without declaring FKs: add a semi-join filter in `_appendSignalLog` and `_appendLocationLog`, so orphan rows are dropped one by one and the rest of the batch still commits.

```sql
WHERE vehicle_id IN (SELECT vehicle_id FROM vehicle)
  AND signal IN (SELECT signal FROM signal_spec)
```

With that, one comment in `schema.dart` recording the no-FK decision, and one test (an orphan packet is dropped and its batch-mates are stored), the rules the FKs would give are enforced where it's cheap.

Want me to add those? Or, if you want the FKs declared anyway for the interview, I can do that as a migration, with the batch-failure trade-off above.

### Claude — 2026-09-14T04:59:27.305Z

### Claude — 2026-09-14T04:59:44.116Z
You're right that primary keys and referential integrity are best practice. Integrity is the goal, though, and an FK constraint is only one way to get it. Whether to declare FKs depends on what kind of database you're building.

## What's universal

| Practice | Applies everywhere? | This project |
|---|---|---|
| Every table has a PK | Yes | Done, all 13 tables |
| No orphan rows (referential integrity) | Yes | **Gap**: nothing checks at ingest |
| Natural key vs surrogate id | Depends on the data | Mixed, chosen per table |
| FK *declared in the schema* | Depends on the workload | Not declared |

## Where declared FKs are the norm

OLTP databases that are the system of record: Postgres, MySQL, SQLite in a CRUD app. Examples are orders→customers or invoices→accounts.
- Writes are one row at a time.
- The parent always exists before the child (you create the customer, then the order).
- One bad row fails one request, and the user sees the error and retries.

In that setting FKs cost almost nothing and catch real bugs. Declare them. Skipping FKs there is bad practice.

## Where skipping them is common

- **Analytical/columnar engines** (DuckDB, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift). Snowflake and BigQuery accept FK syntax but don't enforce it. DuckDB enforces FKs, but has no `ON DELETE CASCADE` and can't add an FK to an existing table.
- **Append-only telemetry and event logs.** Data arrives in batches, one set-based insert per batch, at high volume.
- **Offline-first / sync systems.** Arrival order isn't guaranteed: a reading can land before its vehicle row syncs. A declared FK rejects data that is valid, just early.

This project is all three: DuckDB, a telemetry log, local-first. There the usual practice is:
1. Keep the PKs. Use natural composite keys for time-series rows.
2. Enforce integrity at the ingest boundary: filter orphan rows, count them, surface the count.
3. Write the decision down in the schema.

## Natural vs surrogate PK

Common rule:
- **Entities** get a surrogate id (`vehicle`, `geofence`, `alert`, `trip`).
- **Facts, time-series and junction tables** get a composite natural key (`signal_reading`, `location_fix`, `geofence_containment`, `vehicle_signal_latest`).

The project already follows this. A `signal_reading_id` would go against it: it would allow duplicate readings, so you'd need a unique constraint on the natural key anyway.

## My recommendation

Keep the current keys. Close the integrity gap in the app, and document the no-FK choice. That's the defensible answer for an SDE 3 interview. "I skipped FKs" with no reason sounds careless. "FKs would roll back a whole 500-truck batch because of one early packet, so I filter orphans at the boundary and count them" sounds deliberate.

If the interviewer pushes back, there's a middle option: declare FKs only on the low-volume tables that are always produced by joining the parent (`alert`, `trip`, `geofence_containment`, `ingest_watermark`). They would never fire on the hot ingest path, and the schema would still show the relationships. The catch: on those tables the join already guarantees the parent exists, so the constraints are mostly documentation. Adding them also needs a migration that rebuilds those tables, because DuckDB has no `ALTER TABLE ADD FOREIGN KEY`.

Pick one and I'll build it:
- **A**: ingest orphan filter + schema comment + test (recommended)
- **B**: A, plus declared FKs on the derived tables via a migration
- **C**: declared FKs everywhere, accepting that one bad row fails its whole batch

Future<IngestReceiptModel> _applyBatch(
  Connection conn,
  List<TelemetryPacketModel> batch,
  DateTime now,
) async {
  final stopwatch = Stopwatch()..start();

  await _stage(conn, batch);

  // Transaction 1 — the log and the latest-value table.
  await conn.execute('BEGIN TRANSACTION');
  final int signalsApplied;
  final int locationsApplied;
  try {
    signalsApplied = await _appendSignalLog(conn);
    locationsApplied = await _appendLocationLog(conn);
    await _advanceLatest(conn);
    await conn.execute('COMMIT');
  } catch (_) {
    await conn.execute('ROLLBACK');
    rethrow;
  }

  // Transaction 2 — derivation position. Split from the first so a long
  // recompute never holds a write lock across the whole batch, and so the
  // watermark can only ever lag the log, never lead it (§3.4).
  await conn.execute('BEGIN TRANSACTION');
  final int lateVehicles;
  try {
    lateVehicles = await _countLateVehicles(conn);
    await evaluateAlerts(conn, now);
    await _deriveGeofences(conn);
    await deriveTrips(conn);
    // All of it before the watermark moves. Order matters twice over: the
    // detector reads the *previous* watermark to decide which vehicles have
    // gone backwards and need a full replay, and trips read the containment
    // that same detector has just rewritten.
    await _advanceWatermark(conn);
    await conn.execute('COMMIT');
  } catch (_) {
    await conn.execute('ROLLBACK');
    rethrow;
  }

  final offered = await _stagedCounts(conn);
  return IngestReceiptModel(
    packets: batch.length,
    signalRowsOffered: offered.$1,
    signalRowsApplied: signalsApplied,
    locationRowsOffered: offered.$2,
    locationRowsApplied: locationsApplied,
    lateVehicles: lateVehicles,
    duration: stopwatch.elapsed,
  );
}

/// What one ingest batch actually did.
///
/// The counts are not cosmetic. `offered` minus `applied` is the duplicate
/// count, which is the visible proof that re-delivering a packet is a no-op —
/// the property the whole late/duplicate/out-of-order story rests on (§0).
class IngestReceipt {
  const IngestReceipt({
    required this.packets,
    required this.signalRowsOffered,
    required this.signalRowsApplied,
    required this.locationRowsOffered,
    required this.locationRowsApplied,
    required this.lateVehicles,
    required this.duration,
  });

  /// An empty receipt, for a batch that contained nothing.
  const IngestReceipt.empty()
    : packets = 0,
      signalRowsOffered = 0,
      signalRowsApplied = 0,
      locationRowsOffered = 0,
      locationRowsApplied = 0,
      lateVehicles = 0,
      duration = Duration.zero;

  /// How many packets were in the batch.
  final int packets;

  /// Signal rows the batch contained after de-duplicating within the batch.
  final int signalRowsOffered;

  /// Signal rows that were genuinely new. The rest collided with the natural
  /// key and were dropped by the database, not by application code.
  final int signalRowsApplied;

  final int locationRowsOffered;
  final int locationRowsApplied;

  /// Vehicles in this batch that reported an event time *behind* the position
  /// derivation had already reached. These are the ones whose geofence
  /// transitions and trips will need replaying once derivation exists (§4
  /// step 4). Counted now so the number is visible from the first commit.
  final int lateVehicles;

  /// Wall-clock time the batch took, measured in the writer isolate.
  final Duration duration;

  /// Rows rejected as duplicates — the difference between what was offered
  /// and what the database accepted.
  int get duplicateRows =>
      (signalRowsOffered - signalRowsApplied) +
      (locationRowsOffered - locationRowsApplied);

  @override
  String toString() =>
      'IngestReceipt($packets packets, '
      '${signalRowsApplied + locationRowsApplied} applied, '
      '$duplicateRows duplicates, $lateVehicles late, ${duration.inMilliseconds}ms)';
}

### Claude — 2026-09-14T05:06:13.395Z
Orphan filter, schema comment and test are in. All 273 tests pass and `flutter analyze` is clean. Changes are uncommitted for you to review.

**Filter:** new `_dropOrphans` in [telemetry_writer_isolate.dart](lib/features/telemetry_ingest/data/datasources/telemetry_writer_isolate.dart). It runs right after `_stage` and deletes staged rows whose parent doesn't exist:
- `staging_signal`: vehicle not in `vehicle`, or signal not in `signal_spec`.
- `staging_location`: vehicle not in `vehicle`.

Everything else in the batch reads staging, so one delete there covers all of it: the log, latest values, geofences, trips, the watermark and the late count. A bad row is dropped on its own; the rest of the batch still commits.

**Receipt:** new `orphanRows` field on [ingest_receipt.dart](lib/features/telemetry_ingest/domain/entities/ingest_receipt.dart), shown in `toString`. It defaults to 0, so existing code that builds receipts didn't need changes. Orphans are counted separately, so they don't show up in `duplicateRows`.

**Comment:** added to the doc comment above `migrations` in [schema.dart](lib/db/schema.dart). It records the key rule (natural composite keys for facts, ids for entities and episodes), the logical FKs, why they aren't declared, and where integrity is enforced. I didn't touch the migration SQL itself, since shipped migrations must not change.

**Test:** "orphan rows are dropped without failing the rest of the batch" in [ingest_pipeline_test.dart](test/features/telemetry_ingest/ingest_pipeline_test.dart). One batch holds v1 with a known and an unknown signal, plus an unknown vehicle with a reading and a location. It checks that 3 orphans are counted, v1's `soc` still lands, and no orphan reaches the log, `location_fix`, `vehicle_signal_latest` or `ingest_watermark`.

**The filter caught a bug in an existing test.** "final state is identical however the stream is shuffled or repeated" reopens a fresh database but never re-seeded vehicles, so it had been writing readings for vehicles that don't exist. I pulled the roster into a shared `_fleet` constant and seeded it after the reopen.

The orphan count isn't shown anywhere in the app yet, only on the receipt and in logs. Adding it to the ingest status line would be a small change if you want it.

## AI conversation logs

Deliverable 3, uncurated, in [`ai-logs/`](ai-logs) — full turns, tool calls and
tool results, dead ends included. Regenerate after a session:

```bash
tool/export_ai_logs.sh
```

Claude Code groups transcripts by the directory it was launched from. Sessions
started from a parent directory land in that group next to unrelated work, so
`--src` points at another group and `--match` keeps only this project's
conversations:

```bash
tool/export_ai_logs.sh --src ~/.claude/projects/<group> --match byte_beam_project
```

## Architecture

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Export raw Claude Code session transcripts to ai-logs/*.md (deliverable 3).
# Uncurated: user turns, assistant turns, tool calls and tool results verbatim.
#
#   tool/export_ai_logs.sh                      # sessions run from this project
#   tool/export_ai_logs.sh --src DIR            # also read this transcript dir
#   tool/export_ai_logs.sh --match byte_beam    # only sessions mentioning this
#
# --match exists because Claude Code groups transcripts by the directory it was
# launched from. Sessions for this assignment that were started from a parent
# directory land in that directory's group alongside unrelated work, and only
# this project's conversations belong in this repo.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

SRCS=()
MATCH=""
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --src)   SRCS+=("$2"); shift 2 ;;
    --match) MATCH="$2";   shift 2 ;;
    *) echo "unknown argument: $1"; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done

if [ ${#SRCS[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
  # Claude Code slugs the launch directory; underscores may or may not be folded.
  for SLUG in "$(pwd | sed 's|/|-|g')" "$(pwd | sed 's|[/_]|-|g')"; do
    [ -d "$HOME/.claude/projects/$SLUG" ] && SRCS+=("$HOME/.claude/projects/$SLUG")
  done
fi
[ ${#SRCS[@]} -eq 0 ] && { echo "no transcript directories found"; exit 1; }

mkdir -p ai-logs
python3 - "$MATCH" "${SRCS[@]}" <<'PY'
import json, sys, pathlib

match, srcs = sys.argv[1], [pathlib.Path(p) for p in sys.argv[2:]]
out = pathlib.Path("ai-logs")
CAP = 4000  # tool results are truncated; everything else is verbatim

import 'package:dart_duckdb/dart_duckdb.dart';

import '../../../../core/error/exceptions.dart';
import '../../../../db/vehicle_status_sql.dart';
import '../../domain/entities/fleet_filter.dart';
import '../../domain/entities/fleet_overview.dart';
import '../../domain/entities/vehicle_status.dart';
import '../models/fleet_vehicle_summary_model.dart';

/// Reads the fleet list out of DuckDB.
///
/// The whole read path is `vehicle` (500 rows) joined to
/// `vehicle_signal_latest` (500 x 6) and `signal_spec` (6). No scan of the
/// multi-million-row log happens here, which is the entire reason
/// `vehicle_signal_latest` is maintained on ingest.
abstract class FleetLocalDataSource {
  /// Rows for [filter] plus the count for every chip, read at instant [now].
  Future<FleetOverview> overview(FleetFilter filter, DateTime now);
}

/// DuckDB implementation.
class DuckDbFleetLocalDataSource implements FleetLocalDataSource {
  const DuckDbFleetLocalDataSource(this._read);

  /// The UI isolate's read connection. Sees an MVCC snapshot, so a commit in
  /// the writer never blocks the list.
  final Connection _read;

  @override
  Future<FleetOverview> overview(FleetFilter filter, DateTime now) async {
    try {
      // Two queries, both over the same CTE: the counts must span the whole
      // fleet while the rows are narrowed to one chip. Counting the returned
      // rows instead would make every chip read "the number you can see".
      final counts = await _counts(now);
      final vehicles = await _vehicles(filter, now);
      return FleetOverview(filter: filter, vehicles: vehicles, counts: counts);
    } catch (error) {
      throw LocalDatabaseException('fleet overview query failed', error);
    }
  }

  /// Count per status, plus the total for the "All" chip.
  Future<Map<FleetFilter, int>> _counts(DateTime now) async {
    final result = await _query(fleetCountsQuery, now);

    final counts = {for (final filter in FleetFilter.values) filter: 0};
    var total = 0;
    for (final row in result.fetchAll()) {
      final status = VehicleStatus.fromSql(row[0]! as String);
      final count = (row[1]! as num).toInt();
      total += count;
      counts[_filterFor(status)] = count;
    }
    counts[FleetFilter.all] = total;
    return counts;
  }

  /// The rows for one chip.
  Future<List<FleetVehicleSummaryModel>> _vehicles(
    FleetFilter filter,
    DateTime now,
  ) async {
    final status = filter.status;
    final where = status == null ? '' : "WHERE status = '${status.sqlName}'";
    final result = await _query(fleetRowsQuery(where), now);
    return [
      for (final row in result.fetchAll())
        FleetVehicleSummaryModel.fromRow(row),
    ];
  }

  /// Runs a statement built on [scoredCte], binding the instant to compare
  /// freshness against.
  ///
  /// `now` is bound rather than taken from SQL's own `now()` so tests can pin
  /// it — a fleet list whose rules depend on the wall clock is untestable.
  Future<ResultSet> _query(String sql, DateTime now) async {
    final statement = await _read.prepare(sql);
    try {
      statement.bindParams([now]);
      return await statement.execute();
    } finally {
      await statement.dispose();
    }
  }

  /// Maps a status back to the chip that selects it.
  FleetFilter _filterFor(VehicleStatus status) => switch (status) {
    VehicleStatus.moving => FleetFilter.moving,
    VehicleStatus.idle => FleetFilter.idle,
    VehicleStatus.stopped => FleetFilter.stopped,
    VehicleStatus.offline => FleetFilter.offline,
  };
}

  // buckets duplicating rows that are still live. The CHECKPOINT afterwards is
  // outside it, because it cannot run inside a transaction — and it is the

             count(*),
             min(value),
             max(value),
             avg(value),
             arg_max(value, event_ts)
      FROM signal_reading

      HAVING count(*) > 1

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# dart_duckdb bundles its native library for Android/iOS/macOS app builds, but
# `flutter test` runs on the host Dart VM where nothing has loaded it yet.
# This drops a host dylib in .duckdb/ for test/duckdb_support.dart to point at.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
VERSION="v1.2.1"   # keep in step with dart_duckdb's macos/dart_duckdb.podspec
OUT=".duckdb"
case "$(uname -s)" in
  Darwin) ASSET="libduckdb-osx-universal.zip"; LIB="libduckdb.dylib" ;;
  Linux)  ASSET="libduckdb-linux-amd64.zip";   LIB="libduckdb.so" ;;
  *) echo "unsupported host: $(uname -s)"; exit 1 ;;
esac
[ -f "$OUT/$LIB" ] && { echo "$OUT/$LIB already present"; exit 0; }
mkdir -p "$OUT"
curl -fsSL -o "$OUT/$ASSET" "https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/releases/download/$VERSION/$ASSET"
unzip -oq "$OUT/$ASSET" -d "$OUT" && rm "$OUT/$ASSET"
echo "$OUT/$LIB"

## Dependency pin

`dart_duckdb` is pinned to **1.2.2**, not a caret range. Packages 1.4.1–1.4.4
point their Android Gradle task at GitHub release tags that carry no Android
binaries (`v1.4.1` and `v1.4.4` both 404), so the APK cannot build on them.
1.2.2 downloads from `v1.2.0`, which exists — which is presumably why the brief
names `^1.2.0`. It bundles the DuckDB **1.2.1** engine, so
`tool/fetch_duckdb_lib.sh` fetches that same engine version for host tests.

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dart_duckdb/dart_duckdb.dart';
import 'package:dart_duckdb/open.dart';

/// dart_duckdb loads its native library out of the app bundle on device. Under
/// `flutter test` the host VM has loaded nothing, and the package's own test
/// fallback points at paths inside the dart_duckdb monorepo — so point it at
/// the host copy fetched by `tool/fetch_duckdb_lib.sh`.
///
/// Spawned isolates need no equivalent call: once this isolate has opened the
/// library its symbols are in the process, which is the first thing
/// dart_duckdb looks for.
void useHostDuckDb() {
  final (os, name) = Platform.isMacOS
      ? (OperatingSystem.macOS, 'libduckdb.dylib')
      : (OperatingSystem.linux, 'libduckdb.so');
  final lib = File('.duckdb/$name');
  if (!lib.existsSync()) {
    throw StateError('${lib.path} missing — run tool/fetch_duckdb_lib.sh');
  }
  open.overrideFor(os, lib.absolute.path);
}
